option_description: Controls whether pipelines triggered from forked repositories are permitted to execute with the same privileges and secrets access as pipelines originating from the base or trusted repository. When enabled, external contributors submitting pull requests from forks can have their pipeline code executed in the context of the upstream repository.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires pipeline_definition_untrusted_execution when fork_pipeline_execution_enabled is true and branch_protection_pipeline_review_required is not set, especially if secrets_exposed_to_fork_pipelines is also true. This combination enables supply chain poisoning via T1677 (Poisoned Pipeline Execution) and T1195.001, where an external attacker submits a PR from a fork with a malicious pipeline definition that executes with upstream secrets.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In GitHub, navigate to the repository Settings > Actions > General > Fork pull request workflows section and check whether 'Run workflows from fork pull requests' is enabled and what approval level is set.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Repository > Settings > Actions > General > Fork pull request workflows
how_to_obtain.expected_output: One of: 'Require approval for all outside collaborators', 'Require approval for first-time contributors', or no approval required. If the last option is selected, fork_pipeline_execution_enabled is effectively true.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the GitHub API to retrieve Actions permissions for the repository, which includes fork PR workflow settings.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON response containing 'enabled' and 'allowed_actions' fields; cross-reference with fork workflow approval settings via the Actions API endpoint /repos/{owner}/{repo}/actions/permissions/workflow.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In GitLab, navigate to the project Settings > CI/CD > General pipelines and check the 'Pipelines for Forks' section to see if fork pipelines are enabled.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Project > Settings > CI/CD > General pipelines > Pipelines for Forks
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A toggle indicating whether pipelines from forks are enabled. If enabled, fork_pipeline_execution_enabled is true.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use the GitLab API to retrieve project CI/CD settings and check the allow_fork_pipelines field.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON containing pipeline settings; look for fields related to fork pipeline permissions and protected branch enforcement.

typical_values: true (many open-source projects)
false (recommended for private repositories with secrets)

option_description: Controls whether a human review or approval is mandatory before pipeline definitions from unreviewed or external branches are executed. This acts as a gate preventing untrusted pipeline code (from forks, new contributors, or unprotected branches) from running automatically without any human oversight.
security_impact: The Rego policy for pipeline_definition_untrusted_execution fires in all three of its conditions when branch_protection_pipeline_review_required is not set (i.e., false or absent). This is the single most critical compensating control in the policy — its absence combined with fork execution or an untrusted pipeline definition source creates the poisoned pipeline execution risk (T1677). Without review gates, malicious Jenkinsfile, .github/workflows, or .gitlab-ci.yml changes execute immediately.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In GitHub, navigate to repository Settings > Actions > General and check 'Fork pull request workflows' — verify that 'Require approval for all outside collaborators' or stricter options are selected. Also check Settings > Branches for branch protection rules requiring PR reviews.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Repository > Settings > Actions > General > Fork pull request workflows; Repository > Settings > Branches > Branch protection rules
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Approval requirement set to at least 'Require approval for all outside collaborators', confirming review is required before pipeline execution from forks.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the GitHub Branch Protection API to confirm review requirements are enforced on the default and release branches.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON response with 'required_pull_request_reviews' block present and 'required_approving_review_count' >= 1, confirming review gates are active.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In GitLab, navigate to Settings > CI/CD > Protected branches and verify that pipeline execution on protected branches requires maintainer-level access or approval policies. Also check Settings > CI/CD > Approval rules for pipeline approval requirements.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Project > Settings > CI/CD > Protected Branches; Project > Settings > CI/CD > Approval rules
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Protected branches listed with merge/push access restricted and approval rules showing at least one required approver before pipeline execution.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview the pipeline engineering team to determine whether any automated pipeline execution is permitted from external contributor branches without a designated reviewer approving the workflow run. Check runbooks or contributor guidelines for documented review procedures.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Documented evidence of a mandatory pipeline review step in the contribution process, with a named role responsible for approving external pipeline runs.

typical_values: false (common misconfiguration in open-source and fast-moving teams)
true (security-hardened repositories with external contributor policies)

option_description: Identifies where the pipeline definition file (e.g., .github/workflows/*.yml, .gitlab-ci.yml, Jenkinsfile) is actually loaded from when a pipeline run is triggered — whether from the trusted base repository branch, from a fork or unreviewed contributor branch, or from an unknown/indeterminate source. This is distinct from where the code under test comes from.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires pipeline_definition_untrusted_execution when pipeline_definition_source is 'fork_or_unreviewed_branch' and branch_protection_pipeline_review_required is absent, and also when combined with fork_pipeline_execution_enabled and the source is 'fork_or_unreviewed_branch' or 'unknown'. The critical risk is that the pipeline definition itself contains the commands that execute — sourcing it from untrusted branches means attacker-controlled code runs with upstream credentials, directly enabling T1677 poisoned pipeline execution.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In GitHub Actions, inspect workflow files for use of the 'pull_request_target' trigger combined with a checkout step that references the PR head (github.event.pull_request.head.sha or github.head_ref). This pattern sources pipeline execution context from the fork while running with base repo secrets.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: If 'pull_request_target' is present AND a checkout of the head ref is performed, the pipeline definition source is effectively fork_or_unreviewed_branch. If only 'pull_request' is used, the definition sources from the base.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In GitLab, navigate to Settings > CI/CD and check whether 'Pipelines for Merged Results' is enabled, which uses the pipeline definition from the merged result rather than the fork. Also check if the project uses compliance pipeline templates enforced from a separate trusted project.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Project > Settings > CI/CD > General Pipelines > Pipelines for merged results
how_to_obtain.expected_output: If 'Pipelines for Merged Results' is enabled, the pipeline definition is sourced from the merged target branch (closer to trusted_branch). If disabled with fork pipelines on, source may be fork_or_unreviewed_branch.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Jenkins multibranch pipelines, inspect the Jenkinsfile retrieval configuration to determine whether it reads from the origin branch, a fork branch, or a pinned reference. Check the job configuration XML for SCM configuration.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: SCM configuration showing whether Jenkinsfile is sourced from the originating PR branch (fork_or_unreviewed_branch) or from a pinned trusted branch reference (trusted_branch).

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the CI/CD architecture documentation or interview the DevOps team to determine if a centralized trusted pipeline template mechanism is in place (e.g., GitLab compliance pipelines, GitHub reusable workflows called from a protected ref) that prevents forks from supplying their own pipeline definitions.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Documentation confirming that pipeline definitions are sourced only from protected/trusted branches, or acknowledgment that fork-supplied definitions are permitted.

typical_values: trusted_branch (hardened configurations)
fork_or_unreviewed_branch (open-source projects or misconfigured pull_request_target)
unknown (undocumented or complex multi-repo setups)

option_description: Controls whether CI/CD secrets, tokens, and credentials stored in the pipeline secret management facility are made available as environment variables or injected into pipelines that originate from forked repositories or unreviewed external branches. This is distinct from whether fork pipelines run at all — secrets exposure is the critical escalation factor.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires pipeline_definition_untrusted_execution when secrets_exposed_to_fork_pipelines is true alongside fork_pipeline_execution_enabled and the absence of branch_protection_pipeline_review_required. Exposed secrets in fork pipelines directly enable credential theft (T1552) as an attacker can add a pipeline step to exfiltrate environment variables containing production tokens, deploy keys, or cloud credentials to an external endpoint.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In GitHub Actions, verify that repository secrets are not accessible to workflows triggered by the 'pull_request' event from forks (GitHub blocks this by default). However, check for 'pull_request_target' workflows that explicitly pass secrets using the 'secrets: inherit' directive or explicit secret passing to called workflows.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Repository > Settings > Secrets and variables > Actions; review any workflow files using pull_request_target for 'secrets: inherit' patterns
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Standard 'pull_request' from fork does not receive secrets (secure default). If 'pull_request_target' workflows pass 'secrets: inherit' to called jobs checking out the fork, secrets are exposed — confirm no such pattern exists.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Scan all GitHub Actions workflow files for patterns where secrets are explicitly passed to steps or called workflows within pull_request_target triggered jobs.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -r 'pull_request_target' .github/workflows/ -l | xargs grep -l 'secrets' | xargs grep -E 'secrets\.|secrets: inherit'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: No output indicates secrets are not explicitly passed in pull_request_target workflows. Any matches require manual review to determine if secrets reach code from the fork.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In GitLab, navigate to Settings > CI/CD > Variables and for each variable, check whether 'Protect variable' is enabled. Protected variables are only available to pipelines running on protected branches, preventing exposure to fork pipelines.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Project > Settings > CI/CD > Variables > expand each variable and check 'Protect variable' checkbox status
how_to_obtain.expected_output: All sensitive variables (tokens, keys, passwords) should have 'Protect variable' checked. Any sensitive variable without this flag set is accessible to unprotected branch and potentially fork pipelines.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use the GitLab API to list all project CI/CD variables and check their protected status programmatically.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -H 'PRIVATE-TOKEN: <TOKEN>' 'https://gitlab.example.com/api/v4/projects/<PROJECT_ID>/variables' | python3 -c "import json,sys; vars=json.load(sys.stdin); [print(v['key'], 'protected:', v['protected']) for v in vars]"
how_to_obtain.expected_output: List of all variables with their protected status. Any variable with 'protected: False' containing credentials indicates secrets_exposed_to_fork_pipelines is true.

typical_values: false (GitHub default for standard pull_request trigger)
true (common misconfiguration with pull_request_target or unprotected GitLab variables)
false (GitLab with all variables marked as protected)

option_description: Controls whether the container executing pipeline jobs runs in Docker privileged mode, which grants the container full access to all Linux kernel capabilities, host devices, and removes seccomp/AppArmor restrictions. Privileged mode is commonly used to enable Docker-in-Docker (DinD) builds inside pipeline containers.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires runner_excessive_host_privileges independently whenever privileged_mode_enabled is true, with no additional conditions required. Privileged containers can trivially escape to the host by mounting the host filesystem, modifying kernel parameters, or accessing raw devices, enabling T1611 (Escape to Host) and T1543.005 (Container Service abuse). A compromised build step in a privileged runner can compromise the entire Kubernetes node or Docker host.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For GitLab Runner, inspect the config.toml file on the runner host and look for 'privileged = true' within any [[runners]] block's [runners.docker] section.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output showing 'privileged = false' or absence of 'privileged = true' indicates non-privileged mode. Any 'privileged = true' line confirms the vulnerability.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Kubernetes-based runners (GitLab Runner Helm chart, Tekton, GitHub Actions ARC), inspect the pod security context of runner pods to check for privileged container settings.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output of 'null' or 'false' for all pods indicates non-privileged. Any 'true' value confirms privileged_mode_enabled is true.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Docker-based runners on a host, inspect running containers to check if any runner containers are executing with --privileged flag.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: No output indicates no privileged containers running. Any output showing 'Privileged=true' confirms the misconfiguration.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Kubernetes runner deployments, inspect the Helm values file or runner Deployment/DaemonSet manifest for privileged security context settings.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: securityContext block showing 'privileged: false' or 'runAsNonRoot: true'. Presence of 'privileged: true' confirms the issue.

typical_values: true (Docker-in-Docker build environments, legacy Jenkins agents)
false (rootless Docker builds, Kaniko/Buildah-based image builds)
true (many default GitLab shared runner configurations)

option_description: Enumerates which host Linux namespaces the runner or job container shares with the underlying host node. Host namespaces include hostNetwork (shares host network stack), hostPID (sees all host processes), and hostIPC (accesses host inter-process communication facilities). Each shared namespace progressively reduces container isolation.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires runner_excessive_host_privileges whenever the host_namespace_access array contains any entries (count > 0). hostNetwork enables network sniffing of host traffic and bypasses NetworkPolicy controls; hostPID enables process injection into host processes and secret scraping from /proc/<pid>/environ; hostIPC enables shared memory attacks against other containers. Together they represent T1611 (Escape to Host) enablement without requiring privileged mode.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect all runner pods in the CI/CD namespace for host namespace sharing settings using kubectl.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get pods -n <RUNNER_NAMESPACE> -o json | jq '.items[] | {name: .metadata.name, hostNetwork: .spec.hostNetwork, hostPID: .spec.hostPID, hostIPC: .spec.hostIPC}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON objects with all three fields showing 'false' or 'null' for secure configurations. Any 'true' value for hostNetwork, hostPID, or hostIPC should be recorded in the host_namespace_access array.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the GitLab Runner Helm chart values or Kubernetes manifest for the runner Deployment/DaemonSet to identify any host namespace settings.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: No matches or all values set to 'false'. Any 'true' value confirms that namespace is shared with the host.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Docker-based runners, inspect running runner containers to check for host network mode or other host namespace sharing.
how_to_obtain.command: docker inspect $(docker ps --filter 'name=runner' -q) --format '{{.Name}}: NetworkMode={{.HostConfig.NetworkMode}} PidMode={{.HostConfig.PidMode}} IpcMode={{.HostConfig.IpcMode}}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: NetworkMode should not show 'host'; PidMode should not show 'host'; IpcMode should not show 'host'. Any 'host' values should be added to host_namespace_access.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Jenkins agents running as Kubernetes pods, inspect the pod template configuration in the Jenkins job or shared library for host namespace declarations.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Absence of these fields or explicit 'false' values indicates no host namespace sharing. Present 'true' values identify the namespaces to include in host_namespace_access.

typical_values: [] (properly isolated runners)
['hostNetwork'] (runners needing special network access)
['hostNetwork', 'hostPID'] (severely misconfigured runners)
['hostPID'] (debugging-enabled runner configurations)

option_description: Enumerates specific host filesystem paths that are bind-mounted into the runner or job container, giving the container direct read and/or write access to those locations on the underlying host node. Critical paths include the Docker socket (/var/run/docker.sock), the root filesystem (/), system configuration (/etc), and process information (/proc).
security_impact: The Rego policy fires runner_excessive_host_privileges whenever host_path_mounts contains any entries (count > 0). Mounting /var/run/docker.sock grants full Docker daemon control, enabling container escape by spawning a new privileged container with host mounts — a complete host compromise vector for T1611. Mounting / or /etc allows reading SSH keys, shadow files, and kubeconfig. Mounting /proc enables process memory reading. Any host path mount represents a potential container escape path.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect all runner pods in the CI/CD namespace for hostPath volume mounts, which is the Kubernetes equivalent of host path mounting.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get pods -n <RUNNER_NAMESPACE> -o json | jq '.items[] | {name: .metadata.name, hostPaths: [.spec.volumes[]? | select(.hostPath) | .hostPath.path]}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON showing empty hostPaths arrays for all pods in secure configurations. Any paths listed (especially /var/run/docker.sock, /, /etc) should be recorded in host_path_mounts.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For GitLab Runner with Docker executor, inspect the config.toml volumes section under [runners.docker] for any host path mounts specified with the source:target:mode syntax.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: volumes list should only contain named volumes or cache directories like ['/cache']. Any entry with an absolute host path like '/var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock' or '/:/host' confirms a host path mount.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Docker-based runners, inspect currently running runner containers to enumerate all bind mounts from the host.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output should show no bind mounts from host system paths. Any bind mounts with Source paths starting with /var, /etc, /proc, /sys, or / itself should be included in host_path_mounts.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Search Kubernetes runner Deployment, DaemonSet, or StatefulSet manifests for hostPath volume definitions.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get daemonset,deployment,statefulset -n <RUNNER_NAMESPACE> -o yaml | grep -A 3 'hostPath:' | grep 'path:'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: No hostPath sections present indicates no host path mounts. Any path values returned identify what should be recorded in host_path_mounts (e.g., '/var/run/docker.sock', '/tmp/runner').

typical_values: [] (properly isolated runners)
['/var/run/docker.sock'] (Docker-in-Docker via socket mount — very common and dangerous)
['/var/run/docker.sock', '/cache'] (socket mount with shared cache)
['/'] (catastrophically misconfigured — full host root mount)

option_description: Indicates whether pipeline job containers execute processes as UID 0 (root) inside the container without user namespace remapping. Running as root inside a container is distinct from host root but becomes equivalent to host root when combined with other misconfigurations such as privileged mode or host path mounts, and enables write access to world-writable mounted paths.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires runner_excessive_host_privileges independently whenever runner_run_as_root is true, with no additional conditions required. Root inside a container can exploit kernel vulnerabilities that non-root processes cannot reach, write to host-mounted paths that have root ownership, and abuse setuid binaries within the container image. Combined with any host path mount or privileged mode (also separately detected), root container execution enables complete T1611 (Escape to Host) and T1543.005 exploitation paths.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect runner pod security contexts in Kubernetes to determine the effective UID under which job containers execute.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get pods -n <RUNNER_NAMESPACE> -o json | jq '.items[] | {name: .metadata.name, runAsUser: .spec.securityContext.runAsUser, runAsNonRoot: .spec.securityContext.runAsNonRoot, containerRunAsUser: [.spec.containers[].securityContext.runAsUser]}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Secure configuration shows runAsNonRoot: true or runAsUser set to a value other than 0. If runAsUser is 0, null (defaulting to image USER), or runAsNonRoot is false/absent, runner_run_as_root is likely true.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For actively running pipeline job containers (Docker or Kubernetes), check the actual UID of processes inside the container.
how_to_obtain.command: docker exec $(docker ps --filter 'name=runner' -q | head -1) id 2>/dev/null || kubectl exec -n <RUNNER_NAMESPACE> <RUNNER_POD> -- id
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output showing 'uid=0(root)' confirms runner_run_as_root is true. Output showing a non-zero UID like 'uid=1000(gitlab-runner)' confirms proper non-root execution.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the GitLab Runner config.toml for Docker executor user settings, and check base container images referenced in pipeline definitions for their default USER instruction.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: config.toml should show a non-root user specification. Dockerfiles/pipeline definitions should show 'USER <nonroot>' as the final USER instruction. Absence of explicit user settings typically means root execution.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Kubernetes runners, check if a PodSecurityAdmission policy, OPA/Gatekeeper policy, or Kyverno policy enforces non-root execution in the runner namespace.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get psa,constraint,clusterpolicy -A 2>/dev/null | grep -i 'runner\|ci\|build'; kubectl get namespace <RUNNER_NAMESPACE> -o yaml | grep -A 5 'pod-security'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Presence of a 'restricted' or 'baseline' pod security standard label on the runner namespace, or an active Gatekeeper/Kyverno policy requiring runAsNonRoot, confirms enforcement. Absence means root execution is permitted.

typical_values: true (default for most base images without explicit USER instruction)
true (Jenkins JNLP agents, many GitLab runner images by default)
false (hardened runner images with dedicated non-root service accounts)
false (Kubernetes restricted PSA namespace enforcement)

option_description: Controls whether the CI/CD platform automatically redacts or masks secret values that are injected as environment variables from appearing in build and job logs. When enabled, the platform replaces the literal secret value with a placeholder (e.g., [MASKED]) in any log output where the value would otherwise appear.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires the 'secrets_exposed_in_pipeline_logs' exposure whenever log_masking_enabled is falsy (not input.log_masking_enabled). Without masking, any pipeline step that echoes environment variables, produces verbose output, or runs a tool that prints its configuration will write raw secret values into logs. Combined with a permissive pipeline_log_access_scope, this creates a direct credential theft vector exploiting MITRE T1552 (Unsecured Credentials) and T1654 (Log Enumeration).

how_to_obtain.instruction: In GitLab, navigate to Project → Settings → CI/CD → Variables. Each variable listed as type 'Variable' with the 'Mask' checkbox ticked has masking enabled. Verify ALL secret-type variables have this checked, not just a subset.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Project → Settings → CI/CD → Variables → inspect each variable row for the 'Masked' column checkmark
how_to_obtain.expected_output: All production/sensitive variables show 'Masked: Yes' in the variable list

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the GitLab API for all project-level CI/CD variables and check the masked field on each. Repeat for group-level variables.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Each variable containing a secret value should show '"masked": true'

how_to_obtain.instruction: For GitHub Actions, query the repository secrets list via the GitHub API. Note that GitHub Actions automatically masks all secrets registered via the Secrets store; verify no secrets are stored as plain Variables instead.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: All sensitive values should be registered as Secrets (not Variables); secrets are masked by default in Actions logs

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review Jenkins pipeline definitions and Jenkinsfile scripts for use of the credentials() binding and withCredentials{} blocks. Absence of these wrappers and use of raw environment variables indicates masking is not in effect.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: All secret injection should use withCredentials([]) blocks, not bare env variable assignments

typical_values: true (GitHub Actions default for registered secrets)
false (common in self-managed Jenkins without credentials plugin configuration)
partial (GitLab deployments where some variables lack the Mask checkbox)

option_description: Indicates whether any pipeline step passes secret values directly as command-line arguments (e.g., --password=$SECRET, -p $DB_PASS, curl -u admin:$TOKEN). When secrets appear in command-line arguments, they are visible in process listings (/proc, ps aux), shell history, and often echoed verbatim into logs by shells using xtrace (set -x) or verbose tooling.
security_impact: The Rego policy unconditionally fires 'secrets_exposed_in_pipeline_logs' when secrets_passed_as_plaintext_args is true (input.secrets_passed_as_plaintext_args == true). This is a standalone trigger regardless of log masking status because process-level secret exposure (visible via /proc/PID/cmdline) bypasses platform-level log masking entirely. It maps to MITRE T1552 (Unsecured Credentials) as secrets become recoverable from process tables by any co-tenant process on the runner.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Scan all pipeline definition files for patterns where environment variable references appear inside argument strings for common tools. Look for --token=, --password=, -p , :$, and similar patterns.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Zero matches; any match indicates a secret is being passed as a plaintext argument

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check for shell xtrace (set -x or -x flag in shebang) combined with steps that reference secret environment variables, as xtrace will echo the expanded secret value into logs even if not a direct argument.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: No set -x used in stages that also reference secret variables; if present, ensure those stages are removed or secrets are excluded from that scope

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review recent pipeline execution logs for lines containing recognizable secret patterns. Look for base64-encoded strings, long alphanumeric tokens, or known prefixes (e.g., ghp_, AKIA, glpat-) appearing in command echo lines.
how_to_obtain.command:
# For GitLab, download a recent job log and grep:
curl --header 'PRIVATE-TOKEN: <token>' 'https://gitlab.example.com/api/v4/projects/<id>/jobs/<job_id>/trace' | grep -E '(ghp_|AKIA|glpat-|Bearer [A-Za-z0-9]{20,})'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: No raw credential values appear in log output; [MASKED] placeholders should appear instead

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview pipeline authors and review pipeline coding standards documentation to confirm whether there is a written policy or linter rule prohibiting secrets in command-line arguments, and whether it is enforced in code review.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Written policy exists prohibiting --secret=$VAR patterns; code review checklist includes a secrets-in-args check

typical_values: false (desired state; properly configured pipelines use env vars or stdin)
true (common in legacy pipelines, curl-heavy scripts, and database migration steps using -p flags)
true (frequent in Docker build steps with --build-arg PASS=$SECRET)

option_description: Defines who can read pipeline build logs — controlling whether logs are publicly accessible, visible to all authenticated platform users, restricted to project members, or limited to administrators only. This scope determines the blast radius if secrets are inadvertently written to logs.
security_impact: The Rego policy includes an explicit condition firing 'secrets_exposed_in_pipeline_logs' when log masking is absent AND pipeline_log_access_scope is 'public' or 'all_authenticated_users' (input.pipeline_log_access_scope in ["public", "all_authenticated_users"]). Public log access converts any single secret leak into an externally exploitable credential exposure. Even 'all_authenticated_users' is dangerous in large organizations where any compromised employee account gains access. This feeds MITRE T1654 (Log Enumeration) — attackers specifically hunt pipeline logs for credentials.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In GitLab, navigate to Project → Settings → General → Visibility, project features, permissions. Check the 'Pipelines' visibility setting. Also verify under Settings → CI/CD → General pipelines whether public access is enabled.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Project → Settings → General → Visibility, project features, permissions → Pipelines row
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Pipelines visibility should be set to 'Project Members' or 'Admins' — not 'Everyone' or 'Public'

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the GitLab project API to retrieve the builds_access_level field which controls job log visibility.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'builds_access_level' should be 'private' (project members only) or 'disabled'; combined with 'visibility' not being 'public'

how_to_obtain.instruction: For GitHub Actions, check if the repository is public (which makes all Actions workflow logs publicly readable) and verify the Actions permissions settings.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'private: true' for repositories with sensitive pipelines; public repositories have inherently public logs

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Jenkins, navigate to Manage Jenkins → Configure Global Security → Authorization section. Verify that anonymous users do not have 'Job/Read' permission, which would expose build logs. Check specific job permissions under the job's Configure → Build Permissions.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Manage Jenkins → Configure Global Security → Authorization → Matrix-based security → Anonymous row → Job/Read column
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Anonymous should have no permissions; authenticated users should be limited to project-relevant roles

typical_values: public (common on open-source projects, dangerous if secrets slip into logs)
project_members (typical well-configured private project)
all_authenticated_users (common default in many self-managed GitLab instances)
admins_only (rare, used only for highly sensitive internal tooling)

option_description: Controls whether the package manager and build configuration explicitly resolves dependencies from internal/private registries before attempting public registries. When not enforced, a public registry package with a matching name and higher version number can shadow and replace an internal package, enabling dependency confusion attacks.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires 'dependency_confusion_unvalidated_package_resolution' in two conditions involving registry_precedence_enforced: when both registry_precedence_enforced AND dependency_hash_pinning_enabled are false, and when both registry_precedence_enforced AND public_registry_access_restricted are false. Without precedence enforcement, an attacker who discovers internal package names (via job logs, errors, or source code) can publish a maliciously named package to PyPI/npm/Maven Central at a higher version, which pip/npm/Maven will resolve first, executing attacker-controlled code during builds (MITRE T1195.001).

how_to_obtain.instruction: For pip, check requirements files and pip configuration. Using --extra-index-url adds a public fallback; using --index-url exclusively (no extra-index-url) enforces private-only resolution. Inspect pip.conf and any .pip/pip.conf in the project.
how_to_obtain.command: find . -name 'pip.conf' -o -name '.pip/pip.conf' -o -name 'requirements*.txt' | xargs grep -l 'extra-index-url\|index-url' 2>/dev/null; cat pip.conf 2>/dev/null || cat ~/.config/pip/pip.conf 2>/dev/null
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Should use '--index-url https://private.registry/simple/' with NO '--extra-index-url' pointing to pypi.org; or pip.conf with index-url only

how_to_obtain.instruction: For npm, inspect .npmrc files at project and user level. The registry field should point exclusively to the internal registry with no fallback to registry.npmjs.org.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: registry=https://internal.artifactory.example.com/artifactory/api/npm/npm-virtual/ with no secondary public registry entry

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Maven, inspect settings.xml mirror configuration. A mirror configured with mirrorOf='*' pointing to an internal Nexus/Artifactory blocks all public repository access and enforces internal precedence.
how_to_obtain.command: find ~/.m2 /etc/maven -name 'settings.xml' 2>/dev/null | xargs grep -A5 '<mirrors>'; find . -name 'settings.xml' | xargs grep -A5 '<mirrors>'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: <mirror><mirrorOf>*</mirrorOf><url>https://internal-nexus/repository/maven-public/</url></mirror> with no public Central entry

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect CI pipeline YAML for explicit package manager invocation flags that enforce registry precedence, such as npm install with --registry flag or pip install with --index-url.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: pip install uses --index-url (not --extra-index-url); npm install passes --registry pointing to internal host

typical_values: false (default; most projects use --extra-index-url which still allows public fallback)
false (Maven projects with default Central repository not overridden)
true (organizations using Artifactory/Nexus with enforced mirror-of-all configuration)
true (pip projects using --index-url exclusively without extra-index-url)

option_description: Controls whether all build dependencies are pinned to specific cryptographic hashes in addition to version numbers, ensuring that even if an attacker manages to publish a package at the same version to a public registry, the hash mismatch will cause the build to fail rather than silently install a malicious substitution.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires 'dependency_confusion_unvalidated_package_resolution' in two conditions where dependency_hash_pinning_enabled is false: when combined with absence of registry_precedence_enforced, and when combined with absence of public_registry_access_restricted. Hash pinning is the strongest defense because it is independent of registry routing — even if a confused resolver fetches from the wrong registry, a hash mismatch will abort the build. Without it, version-identical malicious substitutions succeed silently (MITRE T1195.001, T1546.016).

how_to_obtain.instruction: For pip, verify requirements files use hash-checking mode. Each dependency should have --hash=sha256: entries and the file must be invoked with pip install --require-hashes.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Lines like 'requests==2.28.0 --hash=sha256:abc123...' and CI invocation showing pip install --require-hashes -r requirements.txt

how_to_obtain.instruction: For npm, verify package-lock.json exists and contains integrity fields (sha512 hashes) for every dependency. Check that CI runs npm ci (not npm install) which enforces lock file usage.
how_to_obtain.command:
# Check lock file has integrity hashes:
jq '.packages | to_entries[] | select(.value.integrity == null) | .key' package-lock.json | head -20
# Check CI uses npm ci:
grep -rn 'npm ci\|npm install' .github/workflows/ .gitlab-ci.yml Jenkinsfile 2>/dev/null
how_to_obtain.expected_output: jq command returns empty (all packages have integrity hashes); CI uses 'npm ci' not 'npm install'

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Python projects using Pipenv, verify Pipfile.lock exists, is committed to version control, and CI installs with pipenv install --ignore-pipfile to enforce lock file. For Poetry, verify poetry.lock is committed and CI uses poetry install.
how_to_obtain.command: ls -la Pipfile.lock poetry.lock 2>/dev/null; grep -rn 'pipenv install\|poetry install' .gitlab-ci.yml .github/workflows/ Jenkinsfile 2>/dev/null
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Lock file present and committed; CI invokes pipenv install --ignore-pipfile or poetry install (not add)

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Maven, check if maven-enforcer-plugin with requireChecksums or maven-dependency-plugin with verify goal is configured in the POM to enforce artifact hash verification.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: maven-enforcer-plugin configuration with requireChecksums rule present in build lifecycle

typical_values: false (majority of real-world pipelines; npm install without ci, pip without --require-hashes)
true for npm (package-lock.json with integrity is generated by default but only enforced with npm ci)
false for pip (--require-hashes is rarely enabled despite being a pip feature since v8)
true (security-mature organizations with enforced lockfile policies in CI)

option_description: Controls whether the network policy applied to CI/CD runner nodes, or the package manager configuration, blocks direct connections to public package registries (pypi.org, registry.npmjs.org, repo1.maven.org, etc.), forcing all dependency resolution through a controlled internal proxy such as Artifactory, Nexus, or Verdaccio.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires 'dependency_confusion_unvalidated_package_resolution' in two conditions involving public_registry_access_restricted: when combined with absent dependency_hash_pinning_enabled, and when combined with absent registry_precedence_enforced. Network-level restriction is the deepest defense-in-depth control — even misconfigured package manager precedence cannot reach public registries if the network policy blocks the connection. Without restriction, runners can freely fetch from PyPI, npm, or Maven Central, enabling dependency confusion and typosquatting attacks (MITRE T1195.001).

how_to_obtain.instruction: From a pipeline runner environment (or an equivalent container), attempt direct connections to public registry endpoints. A properly restricted environment should timeout or receive a connection refused response.
how_to_obtain.command:
# Run this as a pipeline job step or from the runner container:
curl --max-time 5 -I https://pypi.org/simple/ 2>&1 | head -5
curl --max-time 5 -I https://registry.npmjs.org/ 2>&1 | head -5
curl --max-time 5 -I https://repo1.maven.org/maven2/ 2>&1 | head -5
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Connection timed out or refused for all public registry endpoints; requests to internal proxy succeed

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect Kubernetes NetworkPolicy objects applied to the runner namespace to verify egress rules. Allowlisted egress should only include internal registry hostnames/IPs, not broad 0.0.0.0/0 destinations.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Egress rules list specific internal CIDR blocks or DNS names for the private registry; no 0.0.0.0/0 egress rule exists

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check package manager configuration files in the runner base image or CI job scripts for absence of public registry URLs and presence of internal-only proxy URLs.
how_to_obtain.command:
# Check pip config:
grep -rn 'pypi.org\|pythonhosted.org\|registry.npmjs.org\|repo1.maven.org' .npmrc pip.conf requirements*.txt pom.xml settings.xml 2>/dev/null
# Should return nothing; only internal URLs should appear
how_to_obtain.expected_output: No public registry URLs found in any config file; only internal proxy URLs present

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review cloud provider security group or firewall rules for runner VMs/nodes. Check AWS Security Groups, GCP VPC Firewall rules, or Azure NSGs for egress rules that would permit outbound HTTPS (port 443) to arbitrary internet destinations.
how_to_obtain.command:
# AWS example:
aws ec2 describe-security-groups --group-ids <runner-sg-id> --query 'SecurityGroups[].IpPermissionsEgress[]' --output json | jq '.[] | select(.IpRanges[].CidrIp == "0.0.0.0/0")'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: No egress rule allowing 0.0.0.0/0 on port 443; specific internal CIDR ranges only

typical_values: false (default for most cloud-hosted CI runners; GitHub Actions, GitLab SaaS runners have unrestricted internet access)
false (self-hosted runners without explicit network policy applied)
true (enterprise environments with Artifactory/Nexus acting as the sole registry proxy and firewall egress rules blocking public registries)
partial (Kubernetes-based runners with NetworkPolicy but missing FQDN-based egress controls that still allow public registry IPs)

option_description: Defines the access scope of secrets and credentials stored in the CI/CD platform's secret management facility — specifically whether secrets are available to all pipelines across all branches, restricted to protected branches only, scoped to specific deployment environments, or limited to specific named jobs or stages. This is the primary control for enforcing least-privilege on pipeline credentials.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires 'pipeline_secrets_overprivileged_scope' when secret_scope is 'all_branches' with production_secrets_present true and unprotected branch triggers allowed, and unconditionally when secret_scope is not in the restricted set ['protected_branches_only', 'specific_environments', 'specific_jobs'] while production_secrets_present is true. When secrets are scoped to all_branches, any developer who can create a branch can trigger a pipeline that reads production credentials, enabling lateral movement from development access to production via a modified pipeline step (MITRE T1552, T1555.006).

how_to_obtain.instruction: In GitLab, navigate to Project → Settings → CI/CD → Variables. For each variable, inspect the 'Environment scope' column. 'All (*) ' indicates all_branches scope. Protected variables have the lock icon and 'Protected' flag checked, limiting them to pipelines on protected branches.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Project → Settings → CI/CD → Variables → Environment scope column and Protected checkbox per variable
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Production secrets should show a specific environment scope (e.g., 'production') and have 'Protected' enabled, not 'All (*)'

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the GitLab API to enumerate all project variables and their scopes. Identify any production-named secrets with environment_scope set to wildcard.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Production secrets show environment_scope of a specific environment name (not '*') and protected: true

how_to_obtain.instruction: For GitHub Actions, check that environment secrets are used (not repository-level secrets) for production credentials. Environment secrets require environment protection rules and approval before the job can access them.
how_to_obtain.command:
# List repository secrets (overly broad scope):
gh api repos/{owner}/{repo}/actions/secrets --jq '.secrets[].name'
# List environment-scoped secrets (correct approach):
gh api repos/{owner}/{repo}/environments --jq '.environments[].name' | while read env; do echo "=== $env ==="; gh api repos/{owner}/{repo}/environments/$env/secrets --jq '.secrets[].name'; done
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Production credentials appear only under environment-scoped secrets, not under repository-level secrets

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Jenkins, navigate to Manage Jenkins → Credentials → System. Review each credential's scope (System vs Global) and which folders or pipelines have access. In Declarative Pipelines, check that credentials() references are inside when conditions or specific stage blocks, not at the global environment level.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Manage Jenkins → Credentials → System → Global credentials (unrestricted) vs folder-scoped credentials
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Production credentials stored in folder-scoped credential stores, not in the global credential store accessible to all jobs

typical_values: all_branches (default in GitLab and most CI platforms; broadest exposure)
protected_branches_only (common after basic security hardening; prevents feature branch access)
specific_environments (best practice for production credentials using GitLab environments or GitHub Actions environments)
specific_jobs (rare; achieved via Vault dynamic credentials or per-job IAM role assumption)

option_description: Indicates whether any secrets currently stored in the CI/CD pipeline's secret management store are production-grade credentials — specifically cloud provider access keys, production database passwords, production Kubernetes configs, deployment tokens for production registries, or other credentials that grant access to live production systems rather than test/staging environments.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires 'pipeline_secrets_overprivileged_scope' when production_secrets_present is true combined with either: secret_scope being 'all_branches' with unprotected trigger access, or secret_scope not being in the least-privilege set. The presence of production credentials in a CI/CD system that is broadly accessible dramatically increases the blast radius of any pipeline compromise — a single poisoned job, dependency confusion attack, or log exposure incident results in direct production environment access (MITRE T1552, T1555.006). The pipeline becomes a pivot point from development to production.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In GitLab, navigate to Project → Settings → CI/CD → Variables. Review each variable name against a naming convention for production credentials. Look for prefixes like PROD_, PRODUCTION_, AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID (without staging qualifier), KUBE_CONFIG, DATABASE_URL with production hostnames, or DOCKER_PASSWORD for production registry.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Project → Settings → CI/CD → Variables → review all variable names and descriptions
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Variable names follow environment-qualified naming (STAGING_DB_PASS vs PROD_DB_PASS); production-named secrets flagged for scope review

how_to_obtain.instruction: Enumerate all pipeline variables via API and filter for names matching known production credential patterns. Check for cloud provider key patterns, kubernetes config names, and database URL variables.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Any matches indicate production secrets are present; output should be empty for development-only pipelines

how_to_obtain.instruction: For AWS, verify whether the AWS credentials in the pipeline correspond to production account IAM roles by checking the account ID in the credential context. Production accounts should not have credentials in general-scope pipeline stores.
how_to_obtain.command:
# In a pipeline job, temporarily check which account the credential resolves to:
aws sts get-caller-identity --query '{Account: Account, Arn: Arn}' --output json
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Account ID should match a non-production AWS account number; production account IDs appearing here indicate production credentials are present

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the secrets rotation and provisioning process documentation. Interview the platform team to determine whether production credential provisioning to CI/CD is a controlled exception requiring security approval, or an ad-hoc practice. Check for a secrets inventory register.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Formal process exists requiring security sign-off before production credentials are added to any CI/CD store; inventory register maintained listing all secrets by environment classification

typical_values: true (extremely common; production deployment pipelines routinely store cloud provider keys, kubeconfig, and registry credentials at pipeline level)
true with all_branches scope (frequent anti-pattern found in organizations that grew CI/CD organically without security review)
false (achieved when pipelines use OIDC/Workload Identity Federation to obtain short-lived credentials at runtime instead of storing long-lived keys)
false (organizations using Vault with AppRole or JWT auth where no static secrets are stored in the CI/CD platform itself)

option_description: Controls whether pipeline runs can be triggered from unprotected or feature branches, granting those branch contexts access to the same secrets and permissions as protected branch pipelines.
security_impact: The Rego rule `pipeline_secrets_overprivileged_scope` fires when `unprotected_branch_pipeline_trigger_allowed == true` combined with `secret_scope == all_branches` and `production_secrets_present == true`. Allowing unprotected branch triggers means any developer (or attacker with repository write access) can create a feature branch, modify the pipeline definition to exfiltrate secrets, and trigger execution in a context that has access to production credentials. This is the primary enabler of pipeline poisoning attacks.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect GitHub Actions workflow files for branch filter restrictions on push and pull_request triggers. Absence of a 'branches' filter under 'on:push' means all branches can trigger the workflow.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Secure configuration shows 'branches: [main, release/*]' or equivalent allowlist under each trigger; absence indicates unprotected branches can trigger pipelines.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In GitLab, navigate to the project Settings > CI/CD > Protected Branches. Verify that the relevant pipeline is restricted to run only on branches listed there, and that 'Allow pipelines to run from fork merge requests' is disabled under Settings > CI/CD > General Pipelines.
how_to_obtain.navigation: GitLab Project > Settings > CI/CD > Protected Branches AND Settings > CI/CD > General Pipelines > 'Allow pipelines from fork merge requests'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Production secret scoped variables are marked 'Protected', ensuring they are only exposed on protected branches.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the GitLab API to list protected branches and their pipeline restrictions for the target project, confirming which branches have pipeline execution controls enforced.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A list of protected branch patterns (e.g., 'main', 'release/*'); if empty or missing key branches, unprotected branch triggers are likely permitted.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review Jenkinsfile or Jenkins multibranch pipeline configuration for branch source filtering. Check if the BranchSource is configured with an explicit include pattern restricting builds to protected branches only.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Should show explicit branch include patterns like 'main release/*'; absence means all branches are built.

typical_values: true (common in developer-friendly defaults)
false (hardened/production environments)

option_description: Controls whether cryptographic signing (via Sigstore/cosign, GPG, or Notary) is applied to build artifacts, container images, or binaries before they are promoted between pipeline stages or published to artifact registries.
security_impact: The Rego rule `artifact_integrity_verification_absent` fires when `artifact_signing_enabled` is false (or true without `artifact_hash_verification_enabled`). Without signing, a compromised intermediary pipeline stage, artifact storage system, or registry can substitute malicious artifacts without detection. Signing provides a cryptographic chain of custody linking an artifact to the trusted build process that produced it, blocking supply chain attacks targeting artifact promotion steps.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Search pipeline definition files for signing tool invocations such as cosign, gpg --sign, notation sign, or docker trust sign, and confirm the signing step executes before any promotion or push step.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -rn -E 'cosign sign|gpg --sign|notation sign|docker trust sign|sigstore' .github/workflows/ .gitlab-ci.yml Jenkinsfile 2>/dev/null
how_to_obtain.expected_output: One or more signing commands should appear in a stage that precedes artifact push or environment promotion; absence indicates signing is not implemented.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the container registry (e.g., Docker Hub, AWS ECR, Google Artifact Registry) to check whether image manifests include signature annotations or cosign signature tags (sha256-<digest>.sig).
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Presence of .sig tags and successful cosign verify output indicates signing is active; 'no signatures found' means it is not.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In GitHub, navigate to repository Actions > select a recent successful workflow run > expand the build/publish job steps. Look for a step named 'Sign artifact' or 'cosign sign' in the step list.
how_to_obtain.navigation: GitHub Repository > Actions > [Workflow Run] > [Build/Publish Job] > Step list
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A signing step with exit code 0 should be visible before any deployment or push step.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview the platform engineering or DevSecOps team to determine if a signing key (KMS key, Sigstore OIDC identity, or GPG key) has been provisioned and whether signing is enforced as a pipeline gate that blocks promotion on failure.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Team should be able to identify the signing mechanism, key reference, and confirm that unsigned artifacts cannot be promoted to staging or production registries.

typical_values: false (most organizations lack this control)
true (organizations with mature supply chain security programs using cosign or Notary)

option_description: Controls whether cryptographic hash (SHA-256 or similar checksum) verification is performed when artifacts are pulled from artifact storage or passed between pipeline stages before they are executed or deployed.
security_impact: The Rego rule `artifact_integrity_verification_absent` fires when `artifact_hash_verification_enabled` is false, or when it is true but `artifact_signing_enabled` is false. Hash verification ensures that the artifact consumed in a downstream stage (e.g., deploy) is byte-for-byte identical to what was produced upstream. Without it, a tampered artifact injected into shared storage or passed via an insecure channel can be silently deployed. This is distinct from signing in that hash pinning validates integrity against a known-good value rather than a trusted identity.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect pipeline definition files for checksum validation commands (sha256sum -c, md5sum -c, shasum -a 256) or registry digest pinning (image@sha256:<digest>) in stages that consume artifacts.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Checksum validation commands or digest-pinned image references should appear in deploy/test stages; absence indicates hash verification is not performed.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For package manager dependencies, check lock files (package-lock.json, Pipfile.lock, Cargo.lock, go.sum) to confirm integrity hashes are present and that the pipeline validates them during the build step.
how_to_obtain.command: cat package-lock.json | jq '.packages | to_entries[:5] | .[].value.integrity' 2>/dev/null || grep 'h1:' go.sum | head -5
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Lock files should contain integrity hashes (sha512- prefix for npm, h1: for Go modules); pipeline should run 'npm ci' or 'go mod verify' rather than 'npm install'.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the artifact repository (e.g., Nexus, JFrog Artifactory, GitHub Packages) API to confirm whether artifacts include stored checksums and whether the pipeline job fetches and validates them before use.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Artifact metadata should include SHA-256 values; pipeline scripts should be reviewed to confirm they fetch and compare these values before execution.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review recent pipeline execution logs for checksum validation steps. Look for output lines confirming file hashes match expected values, or for errors indicating hash mismatch failures.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Log lines like 'build.tar.gz: OK' from sha256sum -c, or cosign/notation verification output; absence of any such lines indicates hash verification is not happening.

typical_values: false (default in most CI templates)
true (organizations following SLSA level 2+ requirements or with hardened pipelines)

option_description: Specifies the maximum lifetime in days of static API tokens accepted by the pipeline orchestration API. A value of 0 means tokens are configured to never expire, representing the highest risk configuration.
security_impact: The Rego rule `pipeline_api_authentication_weak` fires when `static_token_lifetime_days > 365` or `static_token_lifetime_days == 0`. Long-lived or non-expiring tokens mean that a compromised credential (via log exposure, repository leak, or phishing) remains valid indefinitely, giving attackers a persistent foothold to trigger pipeline runs or access pipeline APIs. Shorter token lifetimes reduce the window of exploitation and enforce regular credential rotation hygiene.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In GitLab, navigate to Admin Area > Settings > General > Token Lifetime Settings to check the maximum allowed lifetime for personal access tokens and group/project access tokens. In GitHub Enterprise, check Settings > Authentication > Token lifetime policies.
how_to_obtain.navigation: GitLab Admin > Settings > General > 'Personal Access Token prefix' and 'Token lifetime' | GitHub Enterprise Admin > Settings > Personal Access Token policies
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A specific maximum lifetime value (e.g., 90 days) should be configured; 'No limit' indicates tokens can be created without expiry.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use the GitLab API to enumerate existing personal and project access tokens and inspect their expiry dates to identify non-expiring or long-lived tokens in use.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Tokens with 'expires_at: null' or expiry dates more than 365 days in the future indicate policy violations; all tokens should show near-term expiry dates.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query GitHub's organization audit log or token policy API to determine the enforced token expiration policy for the organization, including whether fine-grained token expiration is mandatory.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A JSON object showing a maximum_token_lifetime value in days; absence of the field or a null value indicates no expiration policy is enforced.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the CI/CD secrets inventory or platform team runbook to identify all static tokens in use (Jenkins API tokens, Tekton pipeline tokens, ArgoCD tokens), their creation dates, and whether a rotation schedule is documented.
how_to_obtain.command: jenkins-cli list-credentials --username admin --password <token> -s https://jenkins.example.com/ 2>/dev/null | grep -i token
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Each token should have a documented creation date, rotation schedule, and expiry; Jenkins tokens with no configured expiry are a finding.

typical_values: 0 (non-expiring, common default in self-hosted Jenkins and older GitLab)
90 (compliant SaaS organizations)
365 (commonly selected maximum in less mature environments)
30 (high-security environments)

option_description: Controls whether multi-factor authentication is mandatory for all human user accounts that have permission to trigger or modify pipeline executions, including pushing to branches, approving pipeline runs, or modifying pipeline definitions.
security_impact: The Rego rule `pipeline_api_authentication_weak` fires when `mfa_enforced_for_pipeline_triggers` is false (or absent). Without MFA enforcement, a single compromised password for any account with pipeline write access is sufficient to trigger arbitrary code execution in the pipeline context, including access to all secrets scoped to that pipeline. Given that pipelines execute with elevated privileges and have access to production secrets, account compromise of a developer with pipeline trigger rights is equivalent to production credential exposure.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In GitHub, navigate to Organization Settings > Authentication Security and verify that 'Require two-factor authentication for everyone in the organization' is enabled. Check the list of members without 2FA if the setting shows any non-compliant accounts.
how_to_obtain.navigation: GitHub Organization > Settings > Authentication security > 'Two-factor authentication' enforcement toggle
how_to_obtain.expected_output: The toggle should be enabled and the organization member list should show zero accounts without 2FA configured.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the GitHub API to enumerate organization members and identify those without two-factor authentication enabled, confirming MFA enforcement gaps.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: An empty array indicates all members have MFA enabled; any logins returned represent accounts without MFA that may have pipeline trigger permissions.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the GitLab API for group MFA enforcement settings and identify users within pipeline-relevant groups who do not have MFA configured.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'require_two_factor_authentication: true' with a grace period of 0 indicates full MFA enforcement; 'false' means MFA is optional for group members.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Jenkins environments, review the security realm configuration under Manage Jenkins > Configure Global Security. Check if an SSO/SAML identity provider is configured and whether MFA is enforced at the IdP level for Jenkins access.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Jenkins > Manage Jenkins > Configure Global Security > Security Realm
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Jenkins should be configured to use an external identity provider (SAML/OIDC) where MFA is enforced, rather than Jenkins-native user accounts which lack MFA support.

typical_values: false (common in self-hosted GitLab and Jenkins without SSO)
true (organizations using GitHub.com, GitLab SaaS, or SSO with MFA enforcement)

option_description: Controls whether the pipeline orchestration API validates HMAC signatures on incoming webhook payloads before triggering pipeline runs. When disabled, any party that can reach the webhook endpoint can trigger arbitrary pipeline executions.
security_impact: The Rego rule `pipeline_api_authentication_weak` fires when `webhook_hmac_validation_enabled` is false (or absent). Webhook endpoints without HMAC validation are vulnerable to spoofed trigger events from any network-accessible source. An attacker who can send HTTP POST requests to the webhook URL can trigger pipeline runs, potentially in branches or contexts that expose secrets, without needing any credentials. This is particularly dangerous when combined with broad secret scoping.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In GitLab, navigate to Project Settings > Webhooks and inspect each webhook configuration. Confirm a 'Secret Token' is configured in the webhook definition, which GitLab uses to generate and validate an X-Gitlab-Token header on incoming requests.
how_to_obtain.navigation: GitLab Project > Settings > Webhooks > [Select webhook] > 'Secret Token' field
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Each webhook should have a non-empty Secret Token value; empty secret token fields mean no HMAC validation is performed.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Enumerate project webhooks via the GitLab API and check whether each webhook has a token configured. Webhooks without tokens have no HMAC validation.
how_to_obtain.command: curl --header 'PRIVATE-TOKEN: <admin-token>' 'https://gitlab.example.com/api/v4/projects/<project_id>/hooks' | jq '.[] | {id, url, token: (if .token then "configured" else "MISSING" end)}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: All webhooks should show 'token: configured'; any showing 'token: MISSING' lack HMAC validation and are a security risk.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Attempt to trigger a webhook endpoint without providing a valid HMAC signature (send a POST request with an invalid or missing X-Hub-Signature-256 header) to verify whether the endpoint rejects unauthenticated payloads.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A 403 or 401 HTTP response indicates HMAC validation is enforced; a 200 or pipeline trigger success on an unsigned request indicates validation is absent.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Jenkins with Generic Webhook Trigger plugin, inspect the job configuration XML or Jenkins Configuration as Code (JCasC) YAML to confirm HMAC secret is configured and token-based authorization is required.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Configuration should include a secretToken or hmacSecret element with a non-empty value; absence means webhook triggers are unauthenticated.

typical_values: false (common in Jenkins and self-hosted installations with generic webhook plugins)
true (GitHub Actions, GitLab with properly configured secret tokens, Tekton Triggers with interceptors)

option_description: Controls whether the pipeline API exposes any endpoint capable of triggering a pipeline run without any authentication credential, including no token, no HMAC signature, and no session cookie.
security_impact: The Rego rule `pipeline_api_authentication_weak` fires when `unauthenticated_trigger_allowed == true`. This is the most severe authentication weakness: any party on the network (or internet if the endpoint is publicly exposed) can trigger arbitrary pipeline execution with access to all secrets scoped to that pipeline. This enables trivially launching poisoned pipeline attacks, causing excessive resource consumption, or triggering deployments without any authorization.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Send an unauthenticated HTTP POST request to known pipeline trigger endpoints (e.g., Jenkins build trigger URL, GitLab pipeline trigger URL without token parameter) and observe whether a pipeline run is initiated.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Both requests should return 401 or 403; a 201 or 200 with a pipeline run created indicates unauthenticated triggering is permitted.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Jenkins, navigate to Manage Jenkins > Configure Global Security and verify that 'Allow anonymous read access' is disabled and that all build trigger endpoints require authentication. Check specific job configurations for 'Trigger builds remotely' settings.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Jenkins > Manage Jenkins > Configure Global Security > 'Allow users to sign up' and 'Anonymous' permissions | Job > Configure > 'Trigger builds remotely'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Anonymous role should have no permissions; 'Trigger builds remotely' should either be unchecked or require a token that is validated server-side against authenticated accounts.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the CI/CD platform API without credentials to confirm all pipeline trigger endpoints return authentication errors rather than successfully initiating runs.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: HTTP 401 Unauthorized with '{"message":"401 Unauthorized"}' body confirms authentication is required; any other success response indicates a vulnerability.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review Tekton Triggers EventListener configuration or Argo Events EventSource to confirm all trigger bindings require authentication interceptors (GitHub interceptor, GitLab interceptor, or CEL interceptor with token validation).
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get eventlistener -n tekton-pipelines -o yaml | grep -A5 'interceptors:' | grep -E 'github|gitlab|cel|bitbucket'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Each EventListener should include an interceptor block referencing a secret for HMAC validation; absence of interceptors means events are processed without authentication.

typical_values: false (correct default for most modern CI/CD platforms)
true (legacy Jenkins instances with misconfigured security realm, custom webhook endpoints without auth middleware)

option_description: Controls whether runner registration tokens are periodically rotated on a defined schedule or policy, ensuring that compromised or leaked registration tokens have a limited window of exploitability before they become invalid.
security_impact: The Rego rule `runner_registration_token_unrestricted` fires when `token_rotation_enforced` is false in combination with broad token scope (instance or group level). Runner registration tokens allow any system with the token to register itself as a legitimate pipeline runner. A stolen token without rotation enforcement remains valid indefinitely, allowing an attacker to register a rogue runner that intercepts pipeline jobs, reads environment variables containing secrets, and exfiltrates source code from legitimate pipeline runs without detection.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In GitLab 16+, navigate to Admin Area > CI/CD > Runners. Verify that the legacy static registration token has been disabled and that runner authentication tokens (generated per-runner with expiry) are used instead. Check if token_expiration_limit is configured under Admin > Settings > CI/CD.
how_to_obtain.navigation: GitLab Admin > Settings > CI/CD > 'Runner registration' section | GitLab Admin > CI/CD > Runners > check for legacy token warning banner
how_to_obtain.expected_output: GitLab 16+ should show legacy registration tokens as disabled and all runners should use the new authentication token system with configurable expiry.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the GitLab API to check runner registration token reset history and determine the last time the group or project registration token was rotated, indicating whether rotation is being practiced.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Runners should show recent 'contacted_at' times consistent with active rotation; runners created long ago with no rotation indicate stale tokens.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview the platform or DevOps team to determine if a documented procedure exists for rotating runner registration tokens on a schedule (e.g., quarterly) or in response to security events (e.g., runner compromise, employee offboarding).
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Team should produce a written runbook or automation script (e.g., Terraform plan, Ansible playbook) that rotates runner tokens; inability to produce documentation indicates rotation is ad-hoc or absent.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check infrastructure-as-code or CI/CD platform configuration files for automated token rotation schedules, such as Terraform resources with rotation triggers, Kubernetes CronJobs that invoke token reset APIs, or secrets manager policies with automatic rotation.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Automated rotation logic (scheduled Terraform apply, CronJob manifest, or secrets manager rotation lambda) should be present; absence indicates manual-only rotation with no enforcement.

typical_values: false (most organizations lack formal rotation policy for runner tokens)
true (organizations that have adopted GitLab 16+ runner authentication tokens with expiry, or have automated rotation via Terraform/Ansible)

option_description: Controls whether runner registration tokens are bound to the entire GitLab instance (shared across all groups and projects), scoped to a specific group, or scoped to a specific project. A broader scope means a single stolen token can register a malicious runner against a larger surface area.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires runner_registration_token_unrestricted when token_scope is 'instance' and token rotation is absent or runner_registration_protected is false. Instance-scoped tokens are the most dangerous because a single token compromise allows attacker-controlled runners to intercept jobs across every project on the platform, enabling secret exfiltration and poisoned pipeline execution (T1677, T1528).

how_to_obtain.instruction: In GitLab, navigate to Admin Area > CI/CD > Runners. The presence of a 'Registration token' at the top level confirms instance scope. For group scope, go to a Group > Settings > CI/CD > Runners. For project scope, go to Project > Settings > CI/CD > Runners.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Admin Area > CI/CD > Runners (instance); Group > Settings > CI/CD > Runners (group); Project > Settings > CI/CD > Runners (project)
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A registration token is displayed at the level navigated to, indicating that scope level is active.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the GitLab API to enumerate runners and their type field. 'instance_type' means instance scope, 'group_type' means group scope, 'project_type' means project scope.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON array showing runner_type values; 'instance_type' confirms instance-scoped tokens are in use.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On a self-managed GitLab instance, query the database directly or inspect the application configuration to find where instance-level tokens are defined.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A token string is printed, confirming an instance-level registration token exists and is active.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the gitlab.rb configuration for any forced instance-level runner token settings or inspect the GitLab application settings table for token_scope constraints.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Any explicit token scope overrides or registration token values present in the file.

typical_values: instance
group
project

option_description: Indicates whether registering a new runner requires authorization beyond possessing the registration token—such as admin-only runner creation, IP allowlist enforcement on the registration endpoint, or an approval workflow. When false, anyone who obtains a token can immediately register a runner.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires runner_registration_token_unrestricted when token_scope is 'instance' and runner_registration_protected is false, or when token_scope is 'group' and both token_rotation_enforced and runner_registration_protected are false. Without additional authorization, a leaked token is sufficient for an attacker to register a rogue runner that intercepts jobs and steals secrets (T1677, T1528, T1134).

how_to_obtain.instruction: In GitLab Admin Area, go to Settings > General > 'Sign-up restrictions' or Admin Area > CI/CD and look for any runner approval or IP restriction settings. For GitHub Actions, check Organization Settings > Actions > Runner groups for access controls.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Admin Area > Settings > CI/CD > Runners; check for 'Allow runner registration from' IP restrictions or approval toggles
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Presence of IP allowlist entries or an approval checkbox indicates runner_registration_protected is true.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the GitLab application settings API to check for runner registration restrictions such as runner_registration_token or related protected fields.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Non-null expiration intervals or restriction fields indicate some protection is enforced.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview the platform administrator to determine whether runner registration is restricted to a specific admin role, whether an IP allowlist is enforced on the runner registration endpoint, or whether a manual approval workflow exists before runners are activated.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Confirmation of at least one secondary control (role restriction, IP allowlist, or approval workflow) beyond bare token possession.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Attempt to register a test runner from an IP address outside any documented allowlist using only the registration token, without admin privileges, to verify whether the registration endpoint enforces additional controls.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A '403 Forbidden' or 'registration not allowed' error indicates runner_registration_protected is true; successful registration indicates false.

typical_values: false
true

option_description: Controls whether the pipeline performs cryptographic checksum or signature verification on cache artifacts after they are restored from storage and before their contents are used in the build process. Without this, restored cache contents are trusted implicitly.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires build_cache_poisoning_unverified_restore when cache_integrity_verification_enabled is false and either cache_scope is 'shared' or cache_storage_access_control is 'none' or 'authenticated'. Without integrity checks, an attacker who can write to the cache store can inject malicious compiled objects or dependency files that are silently consumed in subsequent builds, achieving code execution (T1525, T1195.001, T1677).

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect pipeline definition files (.gitlab-ci.yml, Jenkinsfile, .github/workflows/*.yml) for cache restore steps. Look for sha256sum, cosign, or HMAC verification commands executed immediately after cache:restore or actions/cache steps.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Presence of a verification command after cache restore steps confirms integrity verification is enabled.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For GitLab pipelines using the cache keyword, check whether a post-restore job step computes and compares a hash of restored cache contents against a stored manifest.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A verification script line present after the cache restore block indicates integrity checking.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review recent pipeline job logs for cache restore stages and check whether any integrity verification output (e.g., 'SHA256 OK', 'signature verified') appears before the main build step begins.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Log lines showing hash comparison or signature verification output after cache download.
