how_to_obtain.instruction: Ask the pipeline maintainers whether a formal policy exists requiring cache integrity verification and review any pipeline templates or shared CI configuration libraries for verification steps.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Documentation or template code confirming a required verification step in the cache restore process.

typical_values: false
true

option_description: Describes the access control model applied to the shared cache storage backend—whether it is publicly writable with no restrictions ('none'), writable by any authenticated user in the organization ('authenticated'), or writable only by the specific pipeline service account ('pipeline_only').
security_impact: The Rego policy fires build_cache_poisoning_unverified_restore when cache_integrity_verification_enabled is false and cache_storage_access_control is 'none' or 'authenticated'. Overly permissive cache storage means any insider or compromised credential can poison the cache store, injecting malicious artifacts consumed in future builds (T1525, T1195.001, T1677). 'pipeline_only' is the only configuration that meaningfully reduces the blast radius of a credential compromise.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For S3-backed caches, retrieve the bucket ACL and bucket policy to determine who has write access.
how_to_obtain.command: aws s3api get-bucket-acl --bucket <ci-cache-bucket> && aws s3api get-bucket-policy --bucket <ci-cache-bucket> | jq '.Policy | fromjson'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: ACL shows only the pipeline IAM role has write grants; policy denies s3:PutObject from all principals except the runner service account.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For GCS-backed caches, check IAM bindings on the cache bucket to enumerate who holds storage.objects.create or storage.buckets.update roles.
how_to_obtain.command: gsutil iam get gs://<ci-cache-bucket> | jq '.bindings[] | select(.role | contains("storage.objectCreator") or contains("storage.admin"))'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Only the pipeline service account appears in object creator bindings; no allAuthenticatedUsers or allUsers principals.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the runner's config.toml or the CI platform cache backend configuration to identify the storage endpoint and credentials used, then cross-reference with IAM policies.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: The cache section shows a specific service account or access key; validate that account's permissions against the storage backend IAM policy.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In the cloud provider console, navigate to the cache storage bucket (S3, GCS, or Azure Blob) and review the Access Control or Permissions tab to identify any public access grants or broad authenticated-user write permissions.
how_to_obtain.navigation: AWS Console > S3 > <bucket> > Permissions > Bucket ACL and Bucket Policy; GCP Console > Cloud Storage > <bucket> > Permissions
how_to_obtain.expected_output: No public access grants; write permissions limited to a single dedicated service account.

typical_values: none
authenticated
pipeline_only

option_description: Defines how broadly a build cache is shared—whether it is accessible across all branches and pipelines ('shared'), restricted to the originating branch ('branch_scoped'), or created fresh for each pipeline run with no prior cache restoration ('run_isolated').
security_impact: The Rego policy fires build_cache_poisoning_unverified_restore when cache_integrity_verification_enabled is false and cache_scope is 'shared'. A shared cache means a malicious job on any branch can write poisoned artifacts that will be consumed by builds on protected branches, including production deployment pipelines. Broader sharing scope amplifies the impact of a cache poisoning attack (T1525, T1195.001, T1677).

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the pipeline definition file for cache key configuration. In GitLab CI, the cache:key field determines scope—a static key means shared, ${CI_COMMIT_REF_SLUG} means branch-scoped, and absence of cache or key: ${CI_PIPELINE_ID} means run-isolated.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Key using ${CI_COMMIT_REF_SLUG} indicates branch_scoped; ${CI_PIPELINE_ID} or ${CI_JOB_ID} indicates run_isolated; static string or absent key indicates shared.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For GitHub Actions, inspect workflow files for actions/cache steps and examine the key parameter for branch-specific variables versus static strings.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Keys containing github.ref or github.sha indicate branch_scoped or run_isolated; static keys indicate shared scope.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Jenkins pipelines, inspect the Jenkinsfile for cache directives or stash/unstash patterns and determine whether branch name variables are incorporated into cache identifiers.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: BRANCH_NAME or GIT_BRANCH in cache identifiers indicates branch_scoped; absence indicates shared.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In GitLab, navigate to Project > CI/CD > Pipelines, select a recent pipeline, expand a job that uses cache, and review the 'Checking cache for' log line which shows the resolved cache key—this reveals the effective scope.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Project > CI/CD > Pipelines > <pipeline> > <cache job> > Job log > 'Checking cache for' line
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Cache key containing branch name indicates branch_scoped; pipeline/job ID indicates run_isolated; generic name like 'build-cache' indicates shared.

typical_values: shared
branch_scoped
run_isolated

option_description: Controls whether network-level policies (Kubernetes NetworkPolicy, security group egress rules, firewall ACLs, or iptables rules) are applied to runner nodes to restrict their network access exclusively to build-time resources, blocking access to production infrastructure, internal secrets managers, and cloud metadata services.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires network_segmentation_absent_for_runners unconditionally when runner_network_isolation_enforced is false. Without network isolation, a compromised build step or malicious dependency executed in a pipeline job can probe and connect to production databases, internal APIs, and cloud metadata endpoints to harvest credentials and move laterally. This is the primary control preventing build-time compromise from escalating to production compromise (T1072, T1648).

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Kubernetes-hosted runners, list NetworkPolicy resources in the runner namespace and inspect their egress rules to verify production CIDR blocks and metadata IPs are denied.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get networkpolicy -n gitlab-runners -o yaml | grep -A 20 'egress'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Egress rules showing explicit deny or absence of allowances for production subnets (e.g., 10.0.0.0/8) and 169.254.169.254/32.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For EC2-hosted runners, enumerate the security group egress rules attached to runner instances to check for broad 0.0.0.0/0 outbound permissions versus restrictive allowlists.
how_to_obtain.command: aws ec2 describe-security-groups --group-ids $(aws ec2 describe-instances --filters 'Name=tag:role,Values=gitlab-runner' --query 'Reservations[*].Instances[*].SecurityGroups[*].GroupId' --output text) --query 'SecurityGroups[*].IpPermissionsEgress'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Egress rules limited to specific ports/destinations (e.g., 443 to registry and package repo IPs only) rather than 0.0.0.0/0 all-traffic allow.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On runner host nodes, inspect iptables or nftables rules to verify DROP policies for production subnets and the metadata service IP.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: DROP rules present for 169.254.169.254 and known production IP ranges confirm isolation is enforced.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the infrastructure-as-code definitions (Terraform, CloudFormation, Helm charts) for runner nodes to determine whether network policies or security group rules are defined and applied as part of the runner provisioning process.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Explicit deny or restrictive egress rules in IaC code targeting the runner node security boundary.

typical_values: false
true

option_description: Controls whether access to cloud instance metadata services—specifically 169.254.169.254 (AWS/GCP/Azure IMDS) and fd00:ec2::254 (AWS IMDSv2 IPv6)—is explicitly blocked for runner nodes at the network layer, preventing pipeline jobs from obtaining cloud credentials attached to the runner's instance identity.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires network_segmentation_absent_for_runners when both metadata_service_access_blocked and runner_network_isolation_enforced are false. The metadata service is a critical credential theft vector: any code executing in a pipeline job can perform an HTTP GET to 169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/ and obtain the runner instance's IAM role credentials with full cloud API access. SSRF vulnerabilities in build tools make this especially dangerous (T1072, T1648).

how_to_obtain.instruction: From a runner node or a test container in the runner namespace, attempt to reach the metadata service. If the connection is blocked, metadata_service_access_blocked is true.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Connection timeout or 'No route to host' error confirms blocking is in place; successful HTTP 200 response confirms it is not blocked.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On runner host nodes, check for iptables DROP rules targeting the metadata service IP address.
how_to_obtain.command: iptables -L OUTPUT -n | grep 169.254.169.254 && iptables -L FORWARD -n | grep 169.254.169.254
how_to_obtain.expected_output: DROP or REJECT rule for destination 169.254.169.254 confirms the block is enforced at the host firewall layer.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Kubernetes-hosted runners, check for NetworkPolicy egress rules that explicitly deny or omit the link-local metadata range (169.254.0.0/16).
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get networkpolicy -n gitlab-runners -o json | jq '.items[].spec.egress[].to[].ipBlock' | grep -v '169.254'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Absence of 169.254.0.0/16 in any permitted egress ipBlock combined with a default-deny policy confirms blocking.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For AWS environments, verify whether IMDSv2 hop limit is set to 1 on runner EC2 instances, which prevents container workloads from reaching the metadata service through an extra network hop.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: HttpPutResponseHopLimit=1 and HttpTokens=required (IMDSv2 enforced) significantly reduces but does not eliminate metadata access risk from containers.

typical_values: false
true

option_description: Indicates whether runner nodes can establish direct network connections to internal or cloud-hosted secrets management services (e.g., HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, Azure Key Vault, GCP Secret Manager) without going through a controlled pipeline-injection proxy, meaning arbitrary pipeline code can query secrets outside of audited injection mechanisms.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires network_segmentation_absent_for_runners when secrets_manager_reachable_from_runner is true. If a runner can reach the secrets manager directly, any malicious pipeline step or compromised build dependency can enumerate and extract secrets using the runner's attached IAM role or service account credentials—regardless of whether those secrets were intentionally injected into the job. This enables exfiltration of credentials far beyond what the pipeline legitimately needs (T1072, T1648).

how_to_obtain.instruction: From a runner node or test container in the runner execution environment, attempt a TCP connection to the secrets manager endpoint on its service port to verify reachability.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Connection refused or timeout confirms the secrets manager is unreachable from runners; successful connection confirms reachability.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Attempt to call the AWS Secrets Manager API from the runner using the instance's attached IAM role to verify whether the combination of network access and IAM permissions allows secret enumeration.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: An IAM authorization error or network timeout is acceptable; a successful list of secrets confirms runners have unauthorized access.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review egress firewall rules or security group outbound rules on runner nodes to determine whether Vault (port 8200), AWS Secrets Manager (443 to secretsmanager endpoints), or similar services are reachable.
how_to_obtain.command: aws ec2 describe-security-groups --group-ids <runner-sg-id> --query 'SecurityGroups[*].IpPermissionsEgress' | jq '.[][] | select(.ToPort==443 or .ToPort==8200)'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Egress rules showing 0.0.0.0/0 on port 443 without destination prefix list restrictions confirm secrets manager endpoints are reachable.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the runner's network policy or security group IaC definitions to check whether secrets manager endpoints or their CIDR ranges are explicitly excluded from permitted egress destinations.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Explicit deny rules or absence from permitted egress destinations in network policies confirms the secrets manager is blocked.

typical_values: false
true

option_description: Controls whether pipeline execution events—including job triggers, secret access, artifact promotions, and runner registrations—are streamed or forwarded to a centralized audit log system such as a SIEM, S3 bucket, or cloud-native audit service.
security_impact: The Rego rule `pipeline_audit_logging_insufficient` fires immediately when `audit_log_forwarding_enabled` is false, regardless of all other logging settings. Without centralized forwarding, pipeline events exist only in the CI/CD platform's local event store, which is typically accessible to pipeline administrators and can be purged or disabled. This makes forensic reconstruction of malicious pipeline activity—such as unauthorized secret access or rogue runner registration—impossible after the fact.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In GitLab, navigate to Admin Area > Monitoring > Audit Events, then select the 'Streams' tab to verify whether an external streaming destination (HTTP endpoint, AWS S3, or Google Cloud Logging) is configured and active.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Admin Area > Monitoring > Audit Events > Streams
how_to_obtain.expected_output: At least one active streaming destination is listed with a green status indicator.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the GitLab Audit Events streaming API to enumerate configured destinations for the instance.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A non-empty JSON array containing destination objects with `name`, `destination_url`, and `verification_token` fields.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In GitHub Enterprise, navigate to Enterprise Settings > Audit Log > Log Streaming, and check whether a streaming endpoint (AWS S3, Azure Blob, Datadog, Splunk, or custom HTTPS) is configured and verified.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Enterprise Settings > Audit Log > Log Streaming
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A configured and verified streaming destination is displayed with last-delivery timestamp.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Jenkins, verify the Audit Trail plugin is installed and its appenders (SyslogAuditLogger, LogFileAuditLogger forwarding to a remote target) are configured.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: The config.xml contains an `<auditTrail>` block with a `<logBuildCause>true</logBuildCause>` and an active log appender targeting a remote destination.

typical_values: true (enterprise/regulated environments with SIEM integration)
false (default for self-hosted GitLab CE, Jenkins without Audit Trail plugin, small GitHub organizations)

option_description: Controls whether the log destination receiving forwarded pipeline audit events is configured as write-once or immutable storage, preventing any user—including pipeline administrators—from modifying or deleting log entries after they are written.
security_impact: The Rego rule `pipeline_audit_logging_insufficient` fires when `audit_log_forwarding_enabled` is true but `audit_log_immutability_enforced` is false. Even if forwarding is active, a threat actor who compromises a pipeline admin account can delete log entries from a mutable destination to cover tracks before an investigation begins. Immutability ensures the audit trail is tamper-evident and legally defensible.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For an AWS S3 log destination, check whether Object Lock is enabled in Compliance or Governance mode on the target bucket.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON response containing `'ObjectLockEnabled': 'Enabled'` and a `Rule` block with `DefaultRetention` specifying mode COMPLIANCE or GOVERNANCE.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For a SIEM destination such as Splunk, verify that the index storing pipeline audit events has a non-zero frozen time and that index deletion requires a secondary approval workflow.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: `frozenTimePeriodInSecs` is greater than the required retention period in seconds; index deletion is blocked by RBAC.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For AWS CloudTrail log file validation (which may serve as the audit log destination), confirm log file validation is enabled on the trail receiving pipeline events.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: `LogFileValidationEnabled` is `true` for the trail associated with pipeline audit delivery.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the IAM or RBAC policy attached to the log storage service. Confirm that no pipeline service accounts or CI/CD admin roles have `s3:DeleteObject`, `s3:PutBucketObjectLockConfiguration`, or equivalent destructive permissions on the audit log bucket or index.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Simulation result shows `DENY` for all destructive actions against the audit log storage resource.

typical_values: false (default; most teams configure forwarding without separately enabling Object Lock or WORM storage)
true (PCI-DSS, SOC2, or FedRAMP environments with compliance-mandated log retention)

option_description: Enumerates the specific pipeline event categories—such as job_trigger, secret_access, artifact_promotion, runner_registration, and deployment_trigger—that are actively captured and forwarded to the centralized audit log. The completeness of this list determines whether forensically significant events are preserved.
security_impact: The Rego rule `pipeline_audit_logging_insufficient` fires when both `audit_log_forwarding_enabled` and `audit_log_immutability_enforced` are true but neither `secret_access` nor `job_trigger` appears in `audited_event_types`. This means a pipeline logging setup that captures only deployment events would still trigger the finding. Missing `secret_access` events are particularly dangerous because credential theft via pipeline jobs would leave no audit trail.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In GitLab, navigate to Admin Area > Monitoring > Audit Events and review the audit event categories visible in the event stream. Cross-reference against the full list of auditable event types in the GitLab documentation to identify gaps.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Admin Area > Monitoring > Audit Events
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Events visible in the stream include CI/CD job events, secret variable access, runner registration events, and artifact download events.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Retrieve recent audit events from the GitLab API and extract the distinct `entity_type` and `event_name` values to determine which event categories are actively generated and forwarded.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Array includes values such as `ci_build_created`, `ci_variable_accessed`, `runner_registered`, `artifact_download`, and `deploy_token_created`.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For GitHub Enterprise, query the audit log API filtering by CI/CD-related event categories to verify which actions are being recorded.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Array includes `workflows.completed_workflow_run`, `secret.access`, `environment.add_protection_rule`, and similar pipeline lifecycle events.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In the SIEM receiving forwarded pipeline logs, run a frequency analysis on ingested pipeline audit events over the past 30 days to identify event categories present and flag expected categories with zero events.
how_to_obtain.command:
# Splunk SPL example:
index=pipeline_audit sourcetype=gitlab_audit | stats count by event_name | sort -count
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Table shows non-zero counts for job_trigger, secret_access, runner_registration, artifact_promotion, and deployment_trigger event categories.

typical_values: ['job_trigger', 'deployment_trigger'] (common minimal configuration)
['job_trigger', 'secret_access', 'artifact_promotion', 'runner_registration', 'deployment_trigger'] (fully compliant configuration)
[] (no events captured; audit forwarding misconfigured)

option_description: Controls whether the production deployment environment has a mandatory human approval gate enforced—via environment protection rules, required reviewers, or manual pipeline stages—that must be satisfied before any pipeline job can deploy to production.
security_impact: The Rego rule `deployment_approval_gates_bypassed` fires immediately when `production_approval_required` is false, making this the single highest-weight condition in the deployment control policy. Without approval gates, a single compromised pipeline job, poisoned dependency, or malicious PR merge can trigger an automated production deployment with no human checkpoint, directly enabling T1677 (Poisoned Pipeline Execution) and T1072 (Software Deployment Tools) attack techniques.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In GitHub Actions, navigate to Repository Settings > Environments, select the 'production' environment, and verify that 'Required reviewers' is enabled with at least one reviewer or team assigned.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Repository Settings > Environments > production > Environment protection rules
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Required reviewers checkbox is checked and shows one or more named reviewers or teams.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the GitHub API to retrieve the protection rules configured for the production environment and verify required reviewers are present.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON shows `protection_rules` array containing an entry with `type: required_reviewers` and a non-empty `reviewers` list.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In GitLab, navigate to the project's Settings > CI/CD > Protected Environments, verify the 'production' environment is listed as protected, and confirm the 'Required approvals' field is set to 1 or more.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Project Settings > CI/CD > Protected Environments
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'production' environment appears in the protected list with required approval count >= 1 and named approver groups.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the GitLab protected environments API to verify the production environment protection configuration programmatically.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON response with `required_approval_count` >= 1 and a non-empty `approval_rules` array containing valid user or group approvers.

typical_values: false (default in most CI/CD platforms; no protection rules configured on environments)
true (explicitly configured in regulated or mature DevSecOps environments)

option_description: Indicates whether a pipeline job can execute a production deployment automatically—triggered by a merge or push to a protected branch—without passing through an intermediate approval step, environment gate, or promotion workflow.
security_impact: The Rego rule `deployment_approval_gates_bypassed` fires when `production_approval_required` is true but `direct_production_deploy_allowed` is also true, capturing the misconfiguration where approval rules exist in settings but the pipeline definition itself bypasses them (e.g., a `deploy` job with `when: always` targeting production directly after build). This condition allows an attacker who has already satisfied or bypassed branch protection to reach production without triggering an approval workflow.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the pipeline definition file(s) in the repository root. In `.gitlab-ci.yml`, identify any job with `environment: name: production` and check whether `when: manual` or a `needs` dependency on an approval job is absent.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Production deploy job should show `when: manual` or reference an upstream approval job. Absence of either indicates direct deployment is allowed.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For GitHub Actions workflows, inspect `.github/workflows/*.yml` files for jobs that reference the `production` environment and check whether the `environment` block includes a URL but no required reviewer delay.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Jobs targeting production should reference an environment name that has protection rules; absence of `environment: name: production` in the job block means environment gates are not applied.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Jenkins pipelines, review the Jenkinsfile for `stage('Deploy Production')` blocks. Check whether the stage uses an `input` step requiring human confirmation before proceeding.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: An `input` step with a message prompt should appear before any `sh` commands that invoke production deployment tooling.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Trace a recent production deployment in the pipeline execution history. Verify whether any human interaction or approval event appears between the build job completion and the production deploy job start.
how_to_obtain.navigation: CI/CD > Pipelines > [most recent production pipeline] > Job execution timeline
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A manual approval or environment protection gate event is visible in the pipeline timeline between the last build stage and the production deploy job.

typical_values: true (common default in continuous deployment setups and early-stage teams)
false (mature pipelines with explicit manual gates or environment protection rules enforced)

option_description: Counts the number of distinct roles, service accounts, or user identities explicitly granted the ability to override or skip the production approval gate—such as admin bypass lists on protected environments, force-push privileges, or emergency deployment accounts.
security_impact: The Rego rule `deployment_approval_gates_bypassed` fires when `production_approval_required` is true but `approval_bypass_roles_count` exceeds 2, reflecting that more than two bypass identities constitutes an over-privileged bypass surface that undermines the approval gate entirely. Each bypass identity is a potential account compromise vector that eliminates the human checkpoint; a compromised admin or service account in the bypass list can deploy directly to production without triggering an approval workflow.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For GitHub Actions, query the environment's bypass actors list to count the identities granted bypass permissions on the production environment's required reviewer rule.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>' 'https://api.github.com/repos/<owner>/<repo>/environments/production' | jq '[.protection_rules[] | select(.type=="required_reviewers") | .reviewers | length] | add // 0'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: An integer value; cross-reference against the bypass_actors list in the environment settings page to identify which roles can skip approval.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In GitLab, navigate to Project Settings > CI/CD > Protected Environments > production. Expand the 'Allowed to deploy' section and count the number of roles, users, and groups listed. These identities can deploy without waiting for approval if their merge also satisfies branch protection.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Project Settings > CI/CD > Protected Environments > production > Allowed to deploy
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A small list (ideally 0-2 entries) of deployment-authorized identities; large lists or wildcard role assignments indicate excess bypass surface.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use the GitLab API to retrieve the full protected environment configuration and count the combined entries in `deploy_access_levels` that include Maintainer or Owner roles.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Integer count of deploy access level entries; values greater than 2 should be reviewed for least-privilege compliance.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the change management or access control documentation for the production environment. Identify all service accounts used in pipeline automation that have been granted deployment bypass privileges and verify each has a documented business justification.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A documented list of bypass identities with named owners, justifications, and review dates; undocumented entries should be treated as unauthorized.

typical_values: 0 (hardened environments with no bypass permitted)
1-2 (common in teams with a break-glass emergency deployment account)
5-20 (over-privileged configurations where all maintainers or senior engineers have bypass)

option_description: Indicates whether the currently installed CI/CD orchestration platform version (e.g., Jenkins LTS, GitLab Runner, Tekton Pipelines controller, GitHub Actions Runner) has one or more publicly disclosed vulnerabilities in the National Vulnerability Database or vendor security advisory database.
security_impact: The Rego rule `pipeline_orchestrator_patching_deferred` fires when `version_has_known_cve` is true and `days_since_last_patch` is 30 or more. Because the pipeline orchestrator executes arbitrary code, controls secret injection, and communicates with production environments, a known CVE in the orchestrator itself—particularly RCE, authentication bypass, or secrets disclosure classes—gives attackers a direct path to compromise the highest-privilege component in the delivery chain without needing to poison pipeline definitions.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Retrieve the installed Jenkins version and query the NVD API for known CVEs affecting that version.
how_to_obtain.command: JENKINS_VER=$(curl -s -u admin:<token> https://<jenkins_host>/api/json | jq -r '.version') && curl -s 'https://services.nvd.nist.gov/rest/json/cves/2.0?keywordSearch=Jenkins+${JENKINS_VER}&cvssV3Severity=HIGH' | jq '.totalResults'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A count of 0 indicates no high-severity CVEs for that version; any positive number requires immediate review of the CVE list.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use Grype to scan the installed GitLab Runner binary or container image for known CVEs against the NVD and GitHub Advisory Database.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Exit code 0 with 'No vulnerabilities found' or a table of findings; any HIGH or CRITICAL CVE confirms `version_has_known_cve: true`.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the GitLab security advisory feed for the installed GitLab Runner version to check for vendor-disclosed vulnerabilities.
how_to_obtain.command: RUNNER_VER=$(gitlab-runner --version | grep 'Version:' | awk '{print $2}') && curl -s 'https://gitlab.com/api/v4/projects/gitlab-org%2Fgitlab/vulnerability_findings?per_page=20' -H 'PRIVATE-TOKEN: <token>' | jq --arg ver "$RUNNER_VER" '[.[] | select(.location.file | test($ver))]'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Empty array indicates no known vulnerabilities for the installed runner version.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Visit the vendor security advisory page for the installed orchestrator (e.g., https://www.jenkins.io/security/advisories/ for Jenkins, https://about.gitlab.com/releases/categories/releases/ for GitLab) and search for the installed version number to identify any disclosed CVEs.
how_to_obtain.navigation: https://www.jenkins.io/security/advisories/ or https://about.gitlab.com/security/cve/
how_to_obtain.expected_output: No advisory entries list the installed version as affected; if entries exist, record the CVE IDs and CVSS scores.

typical_values: false (current LTS or latest stable release with no outstanding CVEs)
true (installations running end-of-life versions, skipped minor releases, or platforms with deferred patching policies)

option_description: Records the number of calendar days elapsed since the CI/CD orchestration platform was last updated to a newer version, serving as a quantitative measure of patch cadence compliance and the duration of exposure to any vulnerabilities in the previously installed version.
security_impact: The Rego rule `pipeline_orchestrator_patching_deferred` fires when `days_since_last_patch` is 30 or more in conjunction with either `version_has_known_cve: true` or `patching_cadence_policy_defined: false`. A 30-day threshold reflects that publicly disclosed CVEs are actively exploited within days of disclosure; a pipeline orchestrator unpatched for 30+ days during a CVE window represents a high-probability exploitation target given its privileged access to secrets and production systems.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Jenkins installed via package manager on a Debian/Ubuntu host, retrieve the installation or last-upgrade timestamp of the jenkins package.
how_to_obtain.command: grep 'install\|upgrade' /var/log/dpkg.log | grep jenkins | tail -1 | awk '{print $1, $2}' && echo "Days since: $(( ( $(date +%s) - $(date -d "$(grep 'install\|upgrade' /var/log/dpkg.log | grep jenkins | tail -1 | awk '{print $1}')" +%s) ) / 86400 ))"
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A date string and a computed days-since value; values >= 30 trigger the patching policy check.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For a GitLab Runner installed as a Linux package, check the RPM or dpkg installation history to find when the runner package was last upgraded.
how_to_obtain.command:
rpm -q --last gitlab-runner | head -1  # RHEL/CentOS
# OR
zcat /var/log/dpkg.log.* | grep 'gitlab-runner' | grep 'upgrade\|install' | sort | tail -1  # Debian/Ubuntu
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A package name and installation date; compute days since that date to populate this attribute.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the CI/CD platform's own API for version information, then cross-reference against the change management system (e.g., ServiceNow, Jira) for the last approved change record for the orchestrator component.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A version string that can be compared to the change management record's implementation date to calculate elapsed days.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Request the most recent change management ticket or deployment record for the CI/CD orchestrator upgrade from the platform team. The implementation date on the approved change record provides the authoritative patch date for compliance reporting.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A change record with an 'Implemented On' date; subtract from today to obtain the days-since value. If no record exists, treat as unknown and investigate.

typical_values: 0-14 (active patching cadence, automated runner updates enabled)
30-90 (typical for quarterly patch cycles in enterprise environments)
180-365+ (deferred patching, end-of-life versions, or orphaned infrastructure)

option_description: Controls whether a documented and enforced patching schedule exists for CI/CD orchestration components such as Jenkins controllers, GitLab Runners, Tekton controllers, and associated plugins, with a defined maximum interval between patch assessments and application.
security_impact: The Rego rule pipeline_orchestrator_patching_deferred fires when patching_cadence_policy_defined is false and days_since_last_patch is 30 or more. Without a defined policy, the pipeline engine accumulates unpatched CVEs that attackers with job execution access can exploit to escalate privileges or compromise the orchestration layer. The absence of a documented cadence also means enforcement cannot be verified through change management records.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Request the organisation's patch management policy document and search for explicit mention of CI/CD platform components (Jenkins, GitLab Runner, Tekton, GitHub Actions runners). Verify that a maximum patch interval (e.g., 30 days for critical, 90 days for medium) is stated and that CI/CD components are not excluded from scope.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A policy document section explicitly naming CI/CD orchestration components with a defined maximum patch interval and escalation procedure.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review change management records (JIRA, ServiceNow, or equivalent) for patch tickets related to the pipeline orchestration platform over the past six months. Confirm that tickets exist at the cadence stated in the policy and that they are closed within the defined SLA.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Closed change tickets for CI/CD platform patches at the defined interval with completion dates within SLA.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Jenkins: navigate to Manage Jenkins > Plugin Manager > Updates and check the timestamp of the last applied update. For GitLab: navigate to Admin Area > Components and review the last upgrade date recorded in the system information page.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Jenkins: Manage Jenkins > Plugin Manager > Updates | GitLab: Admin Area > System Information
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Last update timestamp that falls within the policy-defined patch interval.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the Jenkins API for installed plugin versions and compare against the known update center manifest to identify plugins with available security updates older than the policy interval.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -u admin:$JENKINS_TOKEN https://jenkins.example.com/pluginManager/api/json?depth=1 | jq '[.plugins[] | select(.hasUpdate==true) | {shortName, version, lastUpdated}]'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Empty array indicates all plugins are current; any entries indicate deferred updates requiring policy review.

typical_values: true (mature organisations with a formal ITSM-backed patch management programme)
false (common in smaller teams or organisations where CI/CD components are treated as developer tooling exempt from IT patch policy)

option_description: Controls whether an explicit egress allowlist or network policy actively restricts outbound traffic from runner nodes during job execution, implemented via Kubernetes NetworkPolicy objects, cloud security group egress rules, or host-based firewall rules that deny traffic to destinations not on the approved list.
security_impact: The Rego rule inter_stage_data_exfiltration_unmonitored fires when egress_network_policy_enforced is false and either egress_traffic_monitoring_enabled is false or runner_network_isolation_mode is shared_unrestricted. Without egress restriction, a malicious build step can POST source code, secrets, or build artifacts to any attacker-controlled endpoint on the internet, constituting automated exfiltration (T1020) or exfiltration over alternative protocol (T1048) with no blocking control.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Kubernetes-hosted runners, list all NetworkPolicy resources in the runner namespace and inspect their egress stanzas to confirm that a default-deny-egress policy exists alongside explicit allow rules for required destinations.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get networkpolicy -n gitlab-runners -o yaml | grep -A 20 'egress:'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: NetworkPolicy with an egress section listing specific ports and CIDR blocks; absence of a policy or a wildcard 0.0.0.0/0 indicates the control is not enforced.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For AWS-hosted runners, query the security groups attached to runner EC2 instances or ECS tasks and inspect egress rules to confirm no rule permits 0.0.0.0/0 on all ports.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Egress rules listing specific port ranges and restricted CIDRs; a rule with IpRanges containing 0.0.0.0/0 and FromPort/ToPort of -1 or 0 indicates unrestricted egress.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect Terraform or CloudFormation infrastructure-as-code files defining runner security groups or Kubernetes NetworkPolicy manifests in the repository to determine whether egress restrictions are codified.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Files containing egress blocks with specific CIDR and port restrictions rather than wildcard allow-all rules.

how_to_obtain.instruction: From an active runner node, attempt a connection to an external endpoint not on the expected allowlist to verify the policy blocks the traffic.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Connection timeout or explicit TCP reset indicating the egress policy is enforced; a successful HTTP 200 response indicates unrestricted egress.

typical_values: false (default in most self-hosted runner deployments where network policy is not configured)
true (Kubernetes environments with a security-conscious platform team or regulated industries)

option_description: Controls whether outbound network traffic originating from runner nodes is captured and logged through a mechanism such as VPC flow logs on the runner subnet, a transparent forward proxy with request logging, DNS query logging via a resolver that captures runner queries, or an IDS/IPS sensor on the runner network segment.
security_impact: The Rego rule inter_stage_data_exfiltration_unmonitored fires when egress_traffic_monitoring_enabled is false combined with either no egress policy or a shared_unrestricted isolation mode. Even when blocking controls are absent, traffic monitoring provides the detection capability needed to identify exfiltration attempts (T1020, T1567.001, T1048). Without this attribute set to true, malicious pipeline jobs can exfiltrate data without any log record being created for forensic reconstruction.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For AWS-based runners, verify that VPC Flow Logs are enabled on the subnet containing runner instances and that logs are being delivered to CloudWatch or S3.
how_to_obtain.command: aws ec2 describe-flow-logs --filter Name=resource-id,Values=$(aws ec2 describe-subnets --filters Name=tag:Name,Values=runner-subnet --query 'Subnets[0].SubnetId' --output text) --query 'FlowLogs[*].{ID:FlowLogId,Status:FlowLogStatus,Destination:LogDestination}' --output json
how_to_obtain.expected_output: At least one flow log entry with FlowLogStatus of ACTIVE; an empty array or INACTIVE status indicates monitoring is not enabled.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Kubernetes runners, check whether a network monitoring tool (Falco, Cilium Hubble, or similar) is deployed in the runner namespace and has visibility into network connections.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep -E 'falco|hubble|cilium' && kubectl exec -n kube-system $(kubectl get pod -n kube-system -l k8s-app=cilium -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}') -- hubble observe --namespace gitlab-runners --last 10 2>/dev/null
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Pods in Running state and observable network events from the runner namespace.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query your SIEM or log aggregation platform for DNS query logs or proxy access logs attributed to runner node IP ranges over the past 7 days to confirm log presence and recency.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Recent DNS query entries attributed to runner IP addresses; no entries may indicate logging is not configured or runners are using a different resolver.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview the platform or security engineering team to confirm whether a forward proxy is deployed for runner egress and whether proxy access logs are retained and reviewed. Request the proxy configuration and a sample log extract.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A proxy configuration file showing runner nodes routed through the proxy and a log retention policy confirming log availability for the required period.

typical_values: false (common in self-hosted environments lacking a dedicated security operations function)
true (cloud-hosted runners where VPC flow logs are enabled as part of a baseline security configuration or where a forward proxy is mandated)

option_description: Classifies the network isolation posture of runner nodes across four tiers: isolated_allowlisted (dedicated subnet with egress restricted to a specific CIDR/port allowlist), isolated_proxy (all egress routes through a logging forward proxy that enforces allowlisting), shared_unrestricted (runners share a network with broad or unrestricted outbound access), or air_gapped (no external internet connectivity permitted).
security_impact: The Rego rule inter_stage_data_exfiltration_unmonitored fires in two of its three conditions when runner_network_isolation_mode is shared_unrestricted. Shared unrestricted mode means build jobs run in the same network context as other workloads and have direct internet access, enabling lateral movement to internal systems and unrestricted data exfiltration. The shared network also allows a compromised build step to reach production infrastructure, cloud metadata services, and internal secrets managers, compounding the impact of other weaknesses.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Kubernetes-hosted runners, identify the namespace and node pool used by runners, then check whether a default-deny NetworkPolicy with explicit egress allowlist entries is applied to that namespace.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get networkpolicy -n gitlab-runners -o json | jq '.items[] | {name: .metadata.name, podSelector: .spec.podSelector, egressRules: .spec.egress}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A policy with egress rules listing specific ports and CIDRs maps to isolated_allowlisted; absence of any policy maps to shared_unrestricted.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For cloud-hosted runners, describe the subnet route table and security group egress rules to determine whether outbound traffic is restricted to a proxy endpoint or specific CIDRs, or whether a default route to the internet gateway exists.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Routes pointing to a NAT gateway or proxy endpoint with no direct internet gateway route indicates isolated_proxy or isolated_allowlisted; a 0.0.0.0/0 route to an internet gateway indicates shared_unrestricted.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the runner deployment Helm values, Terraform module, or Docker Compose file to identify network configuration parameters such as network_mode, subnet assignments, and associated security group references.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Explicit subnet or network references with associated restrictive security group IDs; absence of network restrictions or use of host networking indicates shared_unrestricted.

how_to_obtain.instruction: From a runner node or a test job, attempt connections to several external endpoints and to internal non-build-related services to characterise the actual reachability, independently of the declared configuration.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Both connections timing out indicates air_gapped or isolated mode; success on both indicates shared_unrestricted; success only on the proxy indicates isolated_proxy.

typical_values: shared_unrestricted (default in most self-hosted and many cloud-hosted deployments)
isolated_proxy (common in regulated industries or enterprise environments with a mandatory proxy policy)
isolated_allowlisted (Kubernetes environments with NetworkPolicy enforcement enabled)
air_gapped (rare, typically government or critical infrastructure contexts)

option_description: Indicates whether static analysis or regex pattern scanning of pipeline definition files has identified strings consistent with hardcoded credentials, API keys, tokens, or passwords embedded directly in the file content rather than being supplied via a secrets manager reference.
security_impact: The Rego rule hardcoded_credentials_in_pipeline_definitions fires directly when hardcoded_secret_patterns_detected is true, and fires a second time when it is true and secrets_manager_references_used is also false. Hardcoded secrets in pipeline definitions committed to source control expose credentials to every repository reader, CI system log, and any tooling that processes the repository. This directly realises T1552.001 (Credentials in Files) and provides an attacker with immediate lateral movement capability into any system the credential authenticates to.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Run gitleaks against the repository containing pipeline definition files to detect hardcoded secret patterns across all branches and commit history.
how_to_obtain.command: gitleaks detect --source . --report-format json --report-path gitleaks-report.json --config .gitleaks.toml && cat gitleaks-report.json | jq 'length'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A count of zero indicates no patterns detected; any positive integer requires individual finding review to confirm true positives and set this attribute to true.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Run truffleHog against the repository to scan for high-entropy strings and known secret patterns in pipeline definition files specifically.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: No JSON output indicates no detections; JSON findings with SourceMetadata fields indicate potential hardcoded secrets requiring review.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use grep with a set of common secret patterns to scan pipeline definition files directly for obvious credential assignments.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: No output indicates no obvious patterns; any matched lines require manual review to distinguish true credentials from placeholder or example values.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For GitHub repositories, navigate to the Security tab and review any Secret Scanning alerts that have been raised against pipeline definition files. Filter by file path to focus on workflow and configuration files.
how_to_obtain.navigation: GitHub repository > Security > Secret scanning alerts > Filter by path: .github/workflows
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Active secret scanning alerts with file paths pointing to pipeline definition files indicate hardcoded secrets are present.

typical_values: false (repositories with pre-commit hooks or CI-based secret scanning gates)
true (common in legacy pipelines migrated from other systems or when developers have committed credentials under time pressure)

option_description: Controls whether all credential values in pipeline definition files are supplied exclusively through the platform's secrets manager reference syntax, such as GitHub Actions dollar-double-brace secrets.NAME, GitLab CI masked or protected variable syntax, Jenkins credentials binding plugin references, or Azure Pipelines variable group references, rather than literal plaintext values.
security_impact: The Rego rule hardcoded_credentials_in_pipeline_definitions fires when hardcoded_secret_patterns_detected is true, and the second condition of that rule explicitly checks that secrets_manager_references_used is not true. When this attribute is false, the pipeline definition itself becomes the credential store, meaning any reader of the file or the repository history can extract working credentials. Combined with hardcoded_secret_patterns_detected being true, this creates the highest-confidence signal for T1552 (Unsecured Credentials) and T1552.001 (Credentials in Files).

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect all pipeline definition files and search for environment variable assignments or configuration blocks. Classify each as a secrets manager reference (matching ${{ secrets.* }}, $CI_*, credentials(), or similar) or a literal value.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: No output indicates all credential assignments use reference syntax; any output lines showing literal values indicate secrets_manager_references_used should be set to false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For GitLab CI, use the GitLab API to list all CI/CD variables for the project and confirm that sensitive variables are marked as masked and protected, indicating they are managed through the platform variable store.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: All credential-related variables showing masked: true and protected: true; variables with masked: false containing sensitive names require investigation.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For GitHub Actions, navigate to the repository Settings > Secrets and variables > Actions and confirm that all credential names referenced in workflow files appear as repository or organisation secrets rather than plain environment variables set in the workflow YAML.
how_to_obtain.navigation: GitHub repository > Settings > Secrets and variables > Actions > Repository secrets
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Each credential name used in workflows appears in the secrets list; credential names present only in the workflow YAML as literal values indicate the control is absent.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the Jenkinsfile for use of the credentials() binding syntax and withCredentials blocks to confirm that all sensitive values are bound from the Jenkins credentials store rather than assigned inline.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -n 'withCredentials\|credentials(' Jenkinsfile | wc -l && grep -n 'password\|secret\|token\|key' Jenkinsfile | grep -v 'withCredentials\|credentials(\|\$\|//'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A non-zero count of withCredentials blocks and no literal credential assignments in the second grep output indicates the control is in place.

typical_values: true (pipelines built with platform-native secret management from the outset)
false (common in pipelines with long history, frequent copy-paste from documentation, or pipelines not subject to a secrets management review gate)

option_description: Controls whether all base container image references in pipeline job definitions use immutable SHA256 digest pinning in the format image@sha256:64hexchars rather than mutable tag strings such as latest, stable, or bare semver tags, ensuring that the same image content is pulled on every pipeline execution regardless of upstream registry changes.
security_impact: The Rego rule build_environment_base_image_unpinned fires when image_reference_uses_digest is false. Mutable tags resolve to different image content each time they are pulled; an attacker who compromises the upstream registry or performs a tag reassignment can substitute a malicious image that executes arbitrary code in the build environment on the next pipeline run (T1204.003, T1525). Digest pinning makes image substitution detectable because the registry must serve the exact content matching the declared hash or the pull fails.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Extract all image references from pipeline definition files and check whether each contains the @sha256: digest pattern.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: No output indicates all image references use digest pinning; any output lines reveal mutable tag references that require remediation.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Open each pipeline definition file and manually review every 'image:' directive in GitLab CI job blocks or 'container:' and 'runs-on:' image specifications in GitHub Actions workflow files to confirm the @sha256: suffix is present.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Every matched line contains @sha256: followed by a 64-character hex string; any line with only a tag or no tag indicates unpinned references.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use the Docker registry API or crane tool to resolve the current digest for each image reference found in pipeline files and compare it against any pinned digest to verify pinning is accurate and current.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A sha256: hash that should match the digest in the pipeline definition; a mismatch or the absence of a digest in the pipeline file indicates the attribute should be false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Scan Dockerfile and pipeline YAML files using a dedicated linting tool such as hadolint to detect unpinned base image references.
how_to_obtain.command: hadolint Dockerfile --format json | jq '[.[] | select(.code == "DL3007" or .code == "DL3006")]'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: An empty array indicates no unpinned image findings from hadolint; entries with code DL3007 (using latest tag) indicate the attribute should be false.

typical_values: false (the majority of pipeline definitions in the wild use tag-based references for convenience)
true (security-mature organisations or those implementing SLSA level 2 and above supply chain requirements)

option_description: Contains the list of mutable tag strings identified in base image references across all pipeline job definitions in scope, populated by parsing image: directives and FROM statements and extracting any tag component that does not match the SHA256 digest pattern. Common entries include latest, stable, main, master, edge, nightly, and bare semver strings such as 3.11 or 1.25 without a digest suffix. An empty array indicates no mutable tags were detected.
security_impact: The Rego rule build_environment_base_image_unpinned fires when count(mutable_tag_patterns_found) is greater than zero. Each entry in this array represents a specific image reference that resolves non-deterministically, providing a concrete attack surface for tag reassignment attacks (T1204.003) or registry compromise scenarios (T1525). The list is used in conjunction with image_reference_uses_digest to pinpoint which pipeline jobs and images require remediation rather than requiring assessors to re-scan the repository independently.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Extract all image tag strings from pipeline definition files, filter out SHA256 digest references, and collect the remaining mutable tag values as a unique list.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A list of tag strings such as latest, stable, 3.11, 1.25-alpine; an empty output indicates no mutable tags are present and the attribute should be an empty array.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use the grype or syft tool to parse pipeline definitions and container files, listing image references with their tag resolution type to distinguish digest-pinned from tag-based references.
how_to_obtain.command: syft packages dir:. --scope all-layers -o json 2>/dev/null | jq '[.artifacts[] | select(.type=="docker-image") | .locations[].path + ":" + .version] | unique'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON array of image references; entries without @sha256: in the version field represent mutable tag patterns.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Parse the .gitlab-ci.yml file specifically for the image key at both the global and per-job level, extracting the tag portion from each reference.
how_to_obtain.command:
python3 -c "
import yaml, re, sys
with open('.gitlab-ci.yml') as f:
    doc = yaml.safe_load(f)
pattern = re.compile(r'@sha256:[a-f0-9]{64}$')
tags = []
for k, v in doc.items():
    if isinstance(v, dict) and 'image' in v:
        img = v['image'] if isinstance(v['image'], str) else v['image'].get('name', '')
        if img and not pattern.search(img):
            tag = img.split(':')[-1] if ':' in img else 'no-tag'
            tags.append(tag)
print(list(set(tags)))
"
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A Python list of tag strings found in job image references; an empty list indicates all images use digest pinning.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Run hadolint against all Dockerfiles referenced or used in the pipeline and extract the specific image names and tags flagged by the DL3007 rule (using latest tag) and DL3006 rule (always tag the version of an image explicitly).
how_to_obtain.command: find . -name 'Dockerfile*' | xargs hadolint --format json 2>/dev/null | jq '[.[] | select(.code=="DL3007" or .code=="DL3006") | {file: .file, line: .line, message: .message}]'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON array where each entry identifies a Dockerfile and line with a mutable tag; the tag value from each finding should be added to the mutable_tag_patterns_found list.

typical_values: ['latest'] (single most common finding across public and private repositories)
['latest', 'stable', '3.11', '1.25-alpine'] (typical finding in repositories with multiple pipeline stages and varied base images)
[] (indicates digest pinning is fully applied across all pipeline job definitions)

option_description: Controls whether CI/CD runner environments are single-use and automatically destroyed after each job completes, preventing any state, files, credentials, or environment variables from persisting between separate pipeline job executions.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires runner_job_isolation_disabled when both ephemeral_runners_enforced and workspace_cleanup_enabled are false. Without ephemeral runners, a malicious or compromised job can read artifacts, environment variables, or leftover secrets from a prior job on the same persistent runner host. This enables cross-job data leakage, credential theft, and poisoned pipeline execution (T1677, T1611). Persistent runners also expand the blast radius of a single compromise to all subsequent jobs that land on that host.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the GitLab Runner configuration file for executor type. Ephemeral enforcement is indicated by executor set to 'docker+machine' with autoscaling enabled, or 'kubernetes' with pod-per-job semantics. A plain 'shell' or 'docker' executor without autoscaling is persistent.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Ephemeral: executor = 'docker+machine' with [runners.machine] block present, or executor = 'kubernetes'. Persistent (non-compliant): executor = 'shell' or executor = 'docker' with no autoscaling block.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query all registered GitLab runners via the GitLab API to retrieve their executor type and configuration. Replace GITLAB_URL and TOKEN with your instance values.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON array showing each runner's executor field. Values of 'docker+machine' or 'kubernetes' suggest ephemeral behavior; 'shell' or 'docker' indicate persistent runners.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For GitHub Actions, check whether self-hosted runners are registered as ephemeral using the GitHub API. Ephemeral runners include 'ephemeral' in their labels or are configured via autoscaling solutions like actions-runner-controller with ephemeral=true.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -H 'Authorization: Bearer $GITHUB_TOKEN' -H 'Accept: application/vnd.github+json' 'https://api.github.com/orgs/$ORG/actions/runners?per_page=100' | jq '[.runners[] | {id, name, status, labels: [.labels[].name]}]'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Runner labels list. Presence of 'ephemeral' label or runners showing single-use lifecycle (registration count incrementing per job) confirms ephemeral enforcement.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In GitLab, navigate to Admin Area > CI/CD > Runners and inspect each runner's detail page. For GitHub Actions, navigate to Organization Settings > Actions > Runners and review runner labels and type. Jenkins users should inspect the node/cloud configuration under Manage Jenkins > Manage Nodes and Clouds.
how_to_obtain.navigation: GitLab: Admin Area > CI/CD > Runners > [Select Runner] > Details tab | GitHub: Org Settings > Actions > Runners | Jenkins: Manage Jenkins > Manage Nodes and Clouds > [Cloud Config]
how_to_obtain.expected_output: GitLab: Runner executor shown as 'docker+machine' or 'kubernetes'. GitHub: Runner type listed as 'ephemeral'. Jenkins: Cloud provider (e.g., Kubernetes plugin) configured with pod templates that are discarded after job completion.

typical_values: false (most common — persistent shell or docker executors are the default in self-hosted deployments)
true (GitHub Actions hosted runners are inherently ephemeral; self-hosted deployments using Kubernetes executor or actions-runner-controller with ephemeral mode)

option_description: Controls whether the runner or pipeline configuration explicitly purges the working directory, temporary files, and environment variables between sequential job executions on the same persistent runner host, preventing residual data from one job being accessible to the next.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires runner_job_isolation_disabled when both workspace_cleanup_enabled and ephemeral_runners_enforced are false. On persistent runners, absent workspace cleanup means leftover source code, compiled binaries, injected secrets, and environment variable exports from a previous job remain readable on disk. A subsequent malicious job can harvest these artifacts, enabling credential theft (T1552), cross-job secret leakage, and poisoned pipeline execution (T1677). This is the compensating control for deployments that cannot enforce fully ephemeral runners.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect GitLab Runner configuration for pre_clone_script or pre_build_script hooks that perform workspace wipe, or check for the 'clean_sources' / GIT_CLEAN_FLAGS setting which controls whether git clean is applied before job checkout.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Compliant: pre_clone_script includes 'rm -rf $CI_PROJECT_DIR/*' or GIT_CLEAN_FLAGS = '-ffdx'. Non-compliant: No pre-job cleanup hook and GIT_CLEAN_FLAGS set to 'none' or absent.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review pipeline definition files for explicit cleanup steps at the start of each job or in a global before_script block. Look for workspace wipe commands, rm -rf, or use of platform-provided clean-workspace actions.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Compliant: Evidence of explicit workspace removal commands in before_script/pre-steps, or GIT_CLEAN_FLAGS=-ffdx, or actions/checkout with clean: true. Non-compliant: No cleanup steps found.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Jenkins pipelines, query the Jenkins API for node configurations and check whether the workspace cleanup plugin is installed and applied to jobs. The presence of the ws-cleanup plugin in job configs indicates workspace cleanup is enforced.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -u $JENKINS_USER:$JENKINS_TOKEN '$JENKINS_URL/api/json?tree=jobs[name,url]' | jq -r '.jobs[].url' | while read url; do curl -s -u $JENKINS_USER:$JENKINS_TOKEN "${url}config.xml" | grep -l 'WsCleanup\|cleanWs' && echo "$url: cleanup enabled"; done
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Job config.xml files referencing 'WsCleanup' or 'cleanWs' publisher steps indicate workspace cleanup is configured. Absence across all jobs indicates it is not enforced.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview the CI/CD platform team or review documented runner configuration standards to determine whether a policy mandates workspace cleanup between jobs. Check whether runner registration templates or golden-path pipeline templates include cleanup hooks as a required step.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Review internal IaC runner provisioning templates (e.g., Terraform modules, Helm values for actions-runner-controller) and CI template repositories for mandatory cleanup hooks.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Compliant: Written policy or enforced template requires before_script workspace wipe or platform-level clean flag. Non-compliant: No documented requirement; cleanup is left to individual pipeline authors.

typical_values: false (most common default — GitLab Runner with GIT_CLEAN_FLAGS unset uses fetch strategy which does not fully wipe workspace; Jenkins without ws-cleanup plugin performs no automatic cleanup)
true (explicitly configured via GIT_CLEAN_FLAGS=-ffdx in GitLab, cleanWs() step in Jenkins Declarative pipelines, or actions/checkout with clean: true in GitHub Actions on self-hosted runners)
